Research Proposal: Synthesizing Failure-to-Repair Trajectories for Improving
Code LLM Reasoning## Title
Trajectory-for-Code: Self-Supervised Synthesis of
Debugging Trajectories for Robust Code Generation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current code LLMs are predominantly trained on (instruction,
correct_solution) pairs, either from human sources (e.g., StarCoder data) or
synthetic pipelines (e.g., CodeAlpaca, OSS-Instruct). This outcome-only
supervision has two limitations:

1 Brittle reasoning on hard problems — When the model's first attempt is wrong,
it has no training signal for how to recover. It was never shown buggy
attempts, test failures, or the iterative debugging steps that lead to
correct code.
2 Overconfident generations — Models trained exclusively on correct outputs
lack calibrated uncertainty about when their code is likely wrong, and cannot
self-correct without an external oracle.

Gap: While self-debugging and self-refine methods exist at inference time, no
systematic study has asked whether training on synthesized debugging
trajectories (attempt → test failure → bug analysis → repair → verified fix)
improves a model's code reasoning and self-correction ability at both train and
test time.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary: Fine-tuning a code LLM on self-synthesized debugging
trajectories — sequences where the model sees its own buggy attempt, test
failure signal, natural-language bug explanation, and a corrected solution —
improves pass@1 on held-out reasoning benchmarks by ≥5% over fine-tuning on the
same volume of (instruction, correct_code) synthetic data alone.

Secondary: The same training yields a measurable improvement in self-correction
(ability to improve a generation given test feedback at inference time) without
requiring an external verifier during training.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1 — Trajectory Synthesis Pipeline (fully automated, no human
labels)

Given a base code LLM (e.g., DeepSeek-Coder-7B-Instruct or CodeLlama-7B) and a
set of programming problems from a training split (e.g., APPS training set or a
subset of CodeContests):

1 Attempt: Sample $k=5$ solutions per problem from the model (temperature0.8).
2 Execute: Run each solution against the problem's test cases. Categorize as
pass or fail. Collect the failing test input, expected output, and actual
output.
3 Bug analysis prompt: For each failing solution, prompt the model: "Explain
why this code fails on the given test. Identify the specific bug." This
produces a natural-language bug description. Filter by a lightweight check —
the description must mention the relevant variable or line (heuristic).
4 Repair prompt: Prompt the model: "Given the buggy code, the test failure
details, and the bug explanation above, write a corrected version." Execute
the corrected version; keep only repairs that pass all tests.
5 Assemble trajectory: (problem → buggy_code → test_failure → bug_analysis →
corrected_code). Also include the successful (problem → correct_code) paths
as positive examples.

Yield: ~3–5× more training sequences per problem (one correct path + several
repair trajectories).

To control quality, discard trajectories where:

• The bug analysis is empty or generic (<10 tokens).
• The repair still fails any test case.
• The buggy code has a syntax error (trivial).

Stage2 — TrainingFine-tune the base model on a mixture:

-50% standard (instruction, correct_code) pairs from the same problem set-50%
trajectory data (each trajectory formatted as a multi-turn chat: user → problem,
assistant → code, user → test fails with details, assistant → bug analysis, user
→ fix it, assistant → corrected code)

Train for2 epochs. Use a replay buffer where trajectory data is sampled
proportional to the number of repair steps (more steps → higher weight). Compare
against a control fine-tuned on the same total tokens but only (instruction,
correct_code) pairs.

Stage3 — EvaluationEvaluate on held-out benchmarks (see below). Measure both
static pass@k and self-correction pass@1: allow the model one additional attempt
with test failure feedback.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Training data source:

• CodeContests (training split) ~13K problems with test cases — diverse
difficulty, multiple languages.
• Supplement with APPS (training split) ~5K problems for coverage.

Evaluation benchmarks (held-out, no test set overlap):

• HumanEval+ —164 problems with80× more test cases (EvalPlus). Measures
functional correctness.
• MBPP+ —399 problems with enriched tests.
• LiveCodeBench — recent competitive programming problems, tests recency and
generalization.
• CodeContests (test split) —165 problems.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Description |

|---|---| | pass@1 | Standard functional correctness on first sample
(temperature0.2, greedy) | | pass@5 | Any of5 samples passes (temperature0.8) |
| self-correct pass@1 | First sample + one repair round given test failure
feedback. Measures the model's ability to debug its own output. | | trajectory
efficiency | % of synthesized trajectories that produce valid repairs after one
pass (measures pipeline quality) | | calibration error | Expected Calibration
Error (ECE) on the model's confidence vs. pass rate, to test whether training on
failures produces better-calibrated models |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Base model (no fine-tuning) — e.g., DeepSeek-Coder-7B-Instruct2.
Standard SFT — fine-tuned on (instruction, correct_code) only, matching total
tokens3. Code Alpaca / OSS-Instruct style — synthetic instruction–code pairs
from a teacher model4. Self-play w/o trajectories — generate correct code,
filter by tests, train on that (no failure data)

5 CodeRL baseline — actor-critic with test pass/fail as reward (uses RL, not
SFT on trajectories)
6 Self-Debugging (inference-only, no trajectory training) — to isolate training
benefit---

Ablations1. Remove bug-analysis step: train on (problem → buggy → repair)
without the natural-language bug explanation. Isolates the value of intermediate
reasoning.

2 Remove failure signal: train on (problem → repair) only — show the model the
correct code without showing the failure context.
3 Trajectory ratio sweep: vary the % of trajectory data in the mix
(10%,30%,50%,70%) to measure diminishing returns.
4 Model scale: replicate on1B,7B, and14B models to test whether trajectory
training helps more at smaller scales (where self-correction is hardest).
5 Oracle repair vs. model repair: replace the model's own repair step with
GPT-4's repair to measure the ceiling (is the bottleneck synthesis quality or
training itself?).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation |

|---|---| | Repair data is too easy — the model generates obviously buggy code
that it easily fixes, so trajectories are trivial. | Filter trajectories by the
edit distance of the repair; keep only those with non-trivial changes (>3 tokens
different). | | Model learns to generate buggy code to get repair signal —
exploits the training setup. | Keep the50% standard SFT mix as a regularizer;
never reward buggy-only generations. | | Synthetic bug analysis is hallucinated
— the explanation sounds plausible but is wrong. | The repair step must produce
executed correct code; wrong explanations that still lead to correct repairs are
harmless, and wrong explanations that mislead the repair will be discarded. | |
No improvement on single-turn pass@1 — the benefit only shows in multi-turn
self-correction. | Acceptable if self-correction improves, but the hypothesis
requires ≥5% improvement on pass@1. If self-correction improves without pass@1,
refine the hypothesis. | | Small model can't produce valid bug explanations (<1B
parameters) leads to low-quality trajectories. | Restrict the study to ≥7B
models; use1B as an ablation but expect pipeline yield to be low. | | Metric
saturation — base model is already strong on HumanEval (85%+), leaving little
room. | Use more difficult benchmarks (LiveCodeBench, CodeContests test split)
where scores are lower. HumanEval+ results are still reported but are not the
primary signal. |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SummaryThis proposal tests a simple, automated, and self-supervised method for
creating rich code reasoning data: instead of only generating (problem, answer)
pairs, generate full debugging trajectories — buggy attempt, test feedback, bug
explanation, repair — and train on them. The core idea is that learning how to
recover from failure should produce more robust code reasoning than learning
only from successes. The experiment is feasible with open models, open
benchmarks, and no human annotation.

### 1. Title
**State-Inversion Synthesis: Boosting Code Reasoning via Target-State-to-Code Mapping**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Current synthetic data generation for code Large Language Models (LLMs) primarily follows the "Self-Instruct" paradigm: generating a natural language prompt and then generating the corresponding code. While effective for learning syntax and API usage, this approach often fails to teach models the underlying causal relationship between code execution and memory state. Models frequently hallucinate the outcome of complex loops or pointer manipulations because they treat code as a sequence of tokens rather than a series of state transformations. There is a need for a synthesis method that forces the model to reason backward from a desired execution outcome to the logic required to produce it.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
Training a model on **Inverse State Mapping**—where the input is a specific target memory state (e.g., a complex nested dictionary or a specific heap configuration) and the output is the minimal code required to reach that state from a given input—will result in higher performance on competitive programming benchmarks (e.g., HumanEval, MBPP) than training on standard instruction-to-code pairs.

**Why this is surprising:** Most researchers assume that "intent" (natural language) is the primary signal for code generation. This hypothesis suggests that "state delta" is a more foundational signal for logical reasoning, and that a model can learn general programming logic better by solving "how do I get to this specific memory state?" rather than "how do I solve this word problem?"

### 4. Method
1.  **Seed Program Selection:** Use a small set of high-quality, diverse Python functions from the public domain.
2.  **State Extraction:** Execute these programs using a tracer (like `sys.settrace` or a debugger-like wrapper). At various points in the execution, capture the "State Snapshot": the values of all local and global variables, including complex structures like lists, sets, and objects.
3.  **Synthesis Task Generation:**
    *   **Input:** A "Start State" (e.g., `x = [5, 2, 9]`) and a "Target State" (e.g., `x = [2, 5, 9]`).
    *   **Task:** Generate the Python code (e.g., `x.sort()`) that transforms the Start State into the Target State.
4.  **Teacher Verification:** Use a powerful teacher model (e.g., GPT-4o) to generate multiple candidate solutions for these state-transition tasks.
5.  **Execution Filtering (The "Ground Truth" Filter):** Every synthetic example is executed in a sandbox. If the generated code does not result in the exact Target State when given the Start State, the example is discarded. This ensures 100% label accuracy for the synthetic data.
6.  **Fine-tuning:** Fine-tune a base model (e.g., Llama-3-8B) on these verified (State-In, Code-Out) pairs.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **Training Set:** 50,000 synthetic "State-Inversion" pairs generated from the execution traces of 2,000 seed problems.
*   **Evaluation:**
    *   **HumanEval & MBPP:** To test general coding proficiency.
    *   **CRUXEval:** Specifically designed to test code reasoning and execution simulation.
    *   **LeetCode Hard:** To test complex algorithmic reasoning.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Pass@k:** The standard metric for code generation.
*   **Reasoning Accuracy:** Percentage of cases where the model correctly predicts the output of a code snippet (using the CRUXEval-O benchmark).
*   **State Alignment Score:** A custom metric measuring how close the model's generated code gets to the intended execution state in cases where the code is syntactically correct but logically flawed.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Base Model:** The pre-trained model without fine-tuning (e.g., Llama-3-8B).
*   **CodeAlpaca:** A model fine-tuned on standard instruction-following data.
*   **OSS-Instruct:** A baseline using the "evol-instruct" method of mutating existing code snippets.
*   **Direct Execution Prediction:** Training the model to predict the output of a code snippet (Forward reasoning) rather than the code itself (Inverse reasoning).

### 8. Ablations
*   **State Complexity:** Compare training on simple scalar states (integers/strings) vs. complex data structures (nested JSON/objects).
*   **Verification vs. No Verification:** Compare the performance of the model trained on all teacher-generated code vs. only the code that passed the execution-filter.
*   **State vs. Natural Language:** Mix varying ratios of State-Inversion data with standard instruction-to-code data to find the optimal balance.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **State Explosion:** Randomly generated states might be reachable by infinite variations of code, making the learning signal noisy.
*   **Representation Bottleneck:** Representing a massive heap state in text (JSON-like) might exceed the model's context window or be difficult for the tokenizer to process efficiently.
*   **Overfitting to Short Snippets:** The model might become excellent at "micro-logic" (sorting, filtering) but lose the ability to structure large-scale programs or follow complex natural language requirements.
*   **Feasibility:** Python's execution tracing is mature, making data collection feasible, but the sandbox must be strictly controlled to prevent the execution of malicious or resource-intensive synthetic code.

**Title:** Semantic Context-Aware Speculative Decoding (SCASD): Leveraging Intra-Prompt Redundancy for Drafting

**Problem and Motivation:**
Speculative decoding typically reduces Large Language Model (LLM) inference latency by using a small "drafter" model to predict future tokens, which the larger "target" model then verifies in parallel. However, this approach requires loading a second model into memory, which increases VRAM pressure and introduces synchronization overhead. Furthermore, small drafter models often lack the specific context or "style" of a long prompt, leading to low token acceptance rates in specialized domains (e.g., long-form code generation or legal document analysis).

**Core Hypothesis:**
Large Language Models exhibit high "semantic locality" in long-context inference. I hypothesize that the KV (Key-Value) cache of the current generation contains sufficient structural information to act as its own drafter. Specifically, a lightweight similarity-search mechanism over the existing KV cache can identify recurring patterns to "copy-paste" speculative token sequences, achieving a higher acceptance rate than a generalized small drafter model without the memory overhead of a second model.

**Method:**
1.  **Pattern Identification:** As the target model generates tokens, we monitor the attention heads. When a "trigger" token is generated, we perform a fast k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN) search of the current hidden state against the keys stored in the KV cache.
2.  **Sequence Speculation:** If a high-similarity match is found in the history, the system retrieves the subsequent $N$ tokens that followed that historical match.
3.  **Dynamic Drafting:** These $N$ tokens are treated as the "draft" for the current step.
4.  **Verification:** The target model performs a single forward pass on the $N+1$ tokens (the current token + the draft). Standard speculative verification (e.g., Rejection Sampling) is applied to accept or reject the draft.
5.  **Fallback:** If no high-confidence match is found in the KV cache, the system reverts to standard autoregressive decoding for that step to avoid search overhead.

**Dataset or Benchmark:**
*   **LongBench:** To test performance on long-context retrieval and summarization.
*   **HumanEval / MBPP:** To test structured repetition in code generation.
*   **WikiText-103:** To evaluate general linguistic redundancy.

**Evaluation Metrics:**
*   **Tokens Per Second (TPS):** Primary measure of inference speed.
*   **Speedup Ratio:** TPS (SCASD) / TPS (Standard Autoregressive).
*   **Mean Acceptance Length ($\alpha$):** The average number of tokens accepted per speculative draft.
*   **Memory Overhead:** VRAM usage compared to a standard Drafter-Target model pair.

**Baselines:**
1.  **Standard Autoregressive Decoding:** No speculation.
2.  **Vanilla Speculative Decoding:** Using a small drafter model (e.g., Llama-7B as target, Llama-68M as drafter).
3.  **Medusa:** Multiple-head speculation without a separate drafter model (to compare against internal head-based speculation).

**Ablations:**
*   **Similarity Threshold:** How strict the k-NN match must be to trigger a draft.
*   **Draft Length ($N$):** Testing the optimal number of tokens to "copy" from the KV cache (e.g., 3, 5, or 10 tokens).
*   **Search Frequency:** Comparing searching at every token vs. searching only after specific punctuation or structural markers (e.g., `\n`, `{`, ` `).

**Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks:**
*   **Search Latency:** If the k-NN search over the KV cache is too slow, it may negate the speed gains from parallel verification. This can be mitigated by using FAISS or optimized GPU kernels for similarity search.
*   **Low Redundancy Tasks:** In highly creative or stochastic outputs (e.g., high-temperature poetry), the KV cache may not contain relevant recurring patterns, leading to a 0% acceptance rate and a slight slowdown due to search overhead.
*   **Context Window Limits:** The effectiveness of the method is limited by the size of the KV cache; very short prompts will not have enough history to provide useful drafts.

Research Proposal: Counterfactual Data Augmentation for Mitigating Gender Bias
in Neural Machine Translation## Title
Counterfactual Data Augmentation with
Source-Side Control for Mitigating Occupational Gender Bias in Neural Machine
Translation

Problem
Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models exhibit systematic gender bias:
they disproportionately map neutral-source occupational terms (e.g., "doctor,"
"nurse") to target-language gendered forms that align with statistical
stereotypes rather than real-world distributions. On standard benchmarks like
WinoMT, models such as mBART-50 assign "She is a doctor" the masculine
translation ~85% of the time for English→Spanish, while "nurse" is feminine ~80%
of the time. This propagates occupational stereotypes and can produce
grammatically incorrect output when the context or world knowledge contradicts
the majority pattern.

Existing debiasing approaches fall into three camps — (1) post-hoc decoding
rules, (2) fine-tuning on balanced or anti-stereotypical data, and (3)
embedding-space interventions — but each has limitations: decoding rules can
break fluency, balanced data is scarce and expensive, and embedding
interventions are often task-specific and degrade general translation quality. A
method that requires only synthetic data and a single fine-tuning step, without
specialized architectures or inference-time overhead, would be broadly
applicable across language pairs and model families.

Hypothesis
Adding counterfactually augmented training examples — where
occupational nouns are swapped across genders in the source sentence — combined
with a source-side gender control signal (a special token marking the intended
target gender) will significantly reduce occupational gender bias in NMT output
on WinoMT while preserving BLEU score on standard translation benchmarks
within0.5 points.

The intuition is twofold: (a) the counterfactual data forces the model to learn
that doctor can co-occur with feminine agreement in the target, breaking the
spurious correlation; (b) the control token lets the model disambiguate
ambiguous cases at inference without requiring a separate classifier or post-hoc
rule.

Method1. Counterfactual Data Generation Pipeline

• Start with a parallel corpus (e.g., Europarl + News Commentary for
EN→ES/DE/FR).
• Tag each sentence with occupation-bearing terms using a POS tagger +
occupation lexicon (300 occupation nouns from ONET).
• For each sentence containing an occupational reference to a specific gender
(e.g., "the female doctor"), generate a counterfactual by swapping the gender
descriptor ("the male doctor").
• Also generate sentences where occupation appears without explicit gender
(e.g., "the doctor"), paired with both a masculine and a feminine target
translation obtained by replacing gender-agreement morphology in the
reference.
• Insert a control token at the source sentence head: [GENDER:M], [GENDER:F],
or [NEUTRAL]. The neutral case is used only at inference when gender is truly
unknown.

2. Fine-Tuning

• Mix counterfactual data with original training data at a1:4 ratio (pilot
experiments will test1:1,1:4,1:9).
• Fine-tune a pretrained NMT model (mT5-small or mBART-50) for1–3 epochs with
reduced learning rate (1e-5).
• Evaluate on held-out WinoMT test sets.

3. Inference Protocol

• For sentences where the source has no gender signal, pass the sentence
through a minimal gender-identification classifier (rule-based for EN:
pronoun/coreference heuristics).
• Prepend [GENDER:M] or [GENDER:F] accordingly. When classifier is uncertain,
use [NEUTRAL], which falls back to the most frequent target form.

Dataset / Benchmark- Training corpus: Europarl v7 + News Commentary v12 (EN→ES,
EN→DE, EN→FR; ~2M sentence pairs)

• Counterfactual augmentation: ~50k synthetic sentence pairs generated from the
training corpus- Bias evaluation: WinoMT (Stanovsky et al.,2019) —3,888
pro-stereotype and anti-stereotype sentences covering60 occupations across
EN→ES/DE/FR- General quality evaluation: newstest2013, newstest2014##
Evaluation Metrics| What | Metric | How | |------|--------|-----| | Gender
bias | WinoMT accuracy | % of correct gender assignments for both pro- and
anti-stereotype sentences | | Translation quality | BLEU (sacrebleu) | On
newstest2013/2014 | | Fluency loss | chrF++ | Additional check if BLEU
degrades | | Stereo type flip | Δ between pro- and anti-stereotype accuracy |
Smaller Δ = less biased |

Primary success criterion: WinoMT accuracy on anti-stereotype examples improves
by ≥20 percentage points relative to the baseline, with BLEU drop ≤0.5.

Baselines| Baseline | Description |

|----------|-------------| | Unmodified NMT | mBART-50 fine-tuned on original
data only (no augmentation, no control token) | | Decoding-only | Unmodified
model + gender-inflection post-hoc rule (e.g., adjust target morphology after
decoding) | | Balanced fine-tuning | Fine-tune on a static balanced dataset
(Equalizer, Saunders & Byrne,2020) — no control token | | Embedding debiasing |
Apply Hard Debias (Bolukbasi et al.,2016) to encoder embeddings before
fine-tuning |

Ablations1. No control token: Counterfactual data without [GENDER:M/F] token →
isolates the effect of augmentation vs. control signal.

2 Data ratio sweep:1:1,1:4,1:9 counterfactual-to-original ratio → identifies
trade-off between bias reduction and quality.
3 Occupation-only vs. all-noun augmentation: Only occupations vs. all gendered
nouns → tests whether targeting is necessary or if broader augmentation works
better.
4 Rule-based vs. learned gender classifier at inference: affects how often the
control token is correct.

Expected Failure Modes1. BLEU degradation >0.5: Counterfactual data may distort
the training distribution enough that general translation quality drops.
Mitigation: early stopping based on validation BLEU; fall back to1:9 ratio or
smaller LR.

2 Control token leakage: The model may learn to ignore the token if it's
inconsistently applied (e.g., inference-time [NEUTRAL] differs from training
distribution). Mitigation: include [NEUTRAL] in training on a random10% of
sentences.
3 Language-pair dependence: EN→ES/FR (morphologically gendered
adjectives/determiners) may show larger gains than EN→DE (three-gender system
with more complex agreement). If EN→DE gains are weak, the method may not
generalize to languages with non-binary or richer gender systems.
4 Classifier errors propagate: A bad rule-based gender identifier could prepend
the wrong control token, biasing output in the opposite direction.
Mitigation: measure classifier accuracy; if <80% on a development set, switch
to a lightweight BERT-based classifier.
5 Diminishing returns on larger models: mBART-50 (611M) or mT5-large may
already encode weaker stereotyping at scale. The method may show smaller
gains on larger models — we test on both small and large variants to bound
this.
6 Anti-stereotype improvement does not close the gap: Even with a20pp gain on
anti-stereotype examples, pro-stereotype accuracy may also shift, keeping the
gap large. Success criterion uses the anti-stereotype level rather than Δ
alone for this reason.

### 1. Title
**Neutral-Space Projection: Debiasing Machine Translation via Latent-Space Orthogonalization of Ambiguous Source Embeddings**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Machine Translation (MT) systems frequently exhibit gender bias, typically by defaulting to masculine pronouns for high-status professions (e.g., "The doctor") and feminine pronouns for others (e.g., "The nurse") when translating from gender-neutral languages (like Turkish or Finnish) into gendered ones (like English or Spanish).

Current approaches, such as Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA), require retraining large models on modified datasets, which is computationally expensive and can introduce "over-correction" (e.g., calling everyone "they" even when gender is specified). There is a critical need for a targeted, inference-time or post-hoc intervention that suppresses gendered information *only* when the source context is genuinely ambiguous.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
The "gender" of a noun phrase in a Transformer-based MT model is encoded as a specific, identifiable vector direction within the encoder's latent representations. By identifying this "gender subspace" and projecting encoder hidden states onto its orthogonal complement—specifically when a source sentence lacks explicit gender cues—the decoder will be forced to rely on neutral forms or balanced sampling rather than biased priors, without degrading the overall semantic quality of the translation.

### 4. Method
1.  **Gender Subspace Identification:** Use a small parallel corpus of gendered pairs (e.g., "The actor/The actress") to extract hidden states from the encoder. Apply Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) or Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to identify the primary vector direction ($v_{gender}$) that distinguishes these pairs.
2.  **Ambiguity Detection:** Implement a lightweight "Gender Cues Classifier" that scans the source sentence for explicit gendered markers (names, specific familial terms).
3.  **Latent Projection:** During inference, if the classifier deems the source sentence gender-neutral, the encoder’s final hidden states ($H$) are transformed using a projection matrix $P$:
    $$H_{neutral} = H - (H \cdot v_{gender}) v_{gender}$$
4.  **Decoupled Decoding:** The decoder receives $H_{neutral}$. Because the "gender signal" is removed from the bottleneck, the decoder's cross-attention is forced to utilize the neutral probability space, which can then be steered toward gender-neutral pronouns (e.g., "they") or balanced via beam search.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **Training/Subspace Discovery:** A subset of the **Europarl** or **WMT14** English-French/German datasets.
*   **Evaluation:**
    *   **WinoMT:** A standard benchmark for gender bias in MT consisting of 3,888 sentences where professional nouns must be linked to gendered pronouns.
    *   **MuST-SHE:** A dataset for evaluating gender bias in speech and text translation.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Gender Accuracy:** Percentage of correctly translated pronouns in WinoMT (pro-stereotypical vs. anti-stereotypical).
*   **ΔG (Gender Gap):** The difference in accuracy between masculine and feminine professional translations.
*   **BLEU / ChrF:** To ensure that the latent projection does not destroy the semantic meaning or grammatical fluency of the translation.
*   **Neutrality Score:** Frequency of neutral pronoun usage in ambiguous contexts.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Vanilla Transformer:** A standard Transformer-base model with no debiasing.
*   **CDA (Counterfactual Data Augmentation):** A model retrained on a dataset where "he/she" and "doctor/nurse" pairs are swapped.
*   **Gender-Tagging:** A model where a `<MALE>` or `<FEMALE>` tag is prepended to the source, and a `<NEUTRAL>` tag is used for debiasing.

### 8. Ablations
*   **Projection Strength:** Varying the degree of orthogonalization (partial vs. full projection).
*   **Layer-wise Intervention:** Applying the projection at different layers of the encoder (e.g., only the last layer vs. all layers).
*   **Selective vs. Global:** Applying the projection to all sentences regardless of whether the source is ambiguous.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Semantic Bleeding:** The "gender direction" in the latent space might be entangled with other semantic features (e.g., specific professions). Projecting it out might inadvertently weaken the model's understanding of the profession itself, leading to lower BLEU scores.
*   **Grammaticality in Target:** In highly inflected languages (e.g., Spanish or Arabic), gender affects not just pronouns but also adjectives and verbs. A neutral latent state might lead to "grammatical hallucinations" where the decoder produces inconsistent gender agreements.
*   **Feasibility:** Identifying a single "gender direction" that generalizes across all professions may be difficult; the subspace might be non-linear or manifold-dependent.

Research Proposal: Adaptive Knowledge Injection via Confidence-Gated Adapter
Fusion for Domain-Specific LLMs## Title
Confidence-Gated Adapter Fusion for
Mitigating Knowledge Conflicts During Domain-Specific LLM Injection

Problem
Domain-specific LLM deployment (legal, medical, finance) requires
injecting specialized knowledge into general-purpose pre-trained models. Three
interrelated challenges remain unresolved:

1 Knowledge conflicts — injected domain facts contradict or compete with the
model's pre-training knowledge, causing inconsistent behavior depending on
prompt phrasing.
2 Selective forgetting — fine-tuning on domain text degrades general-language
capabilities, especially on reasoning and rare-token recall.
3 Sub-domain interference — a single domain (e.g., clinical medicine) contains
heterogeneous sub-domains (radiology, pathology, pharmacology) that interfere
when injected via a single adapter or fine-tuning run.

Current solutions (full fine-tuning, RAG, LoRA, model editing) each address only
a subset of these. No method jointly handles all three while providing per-input
routing between base and injected knowledge.

Hypothesis
Confidence-gated routing — where the model dynamically selects between
base knowledge and injected domain knowledge based on its own predictive
uncertainty — reduces knowledge conflicts and sub-domain interference compared
to monolithic injection, while preserving general capabilities better than full
fine-tuning and matching the domain accuracy of state-of-the-art fixed injection
methods.

More concretely: an adapter mixture with a learned confidence-gating mechanism
will achieve higher domain-specific accuracy and lower general-task degradation
than the Pareto frontier of existing injection methods.

Method
Architecture. Start with a frozen base LLM (e.g., Llama-3-8B). We train a
set of k lightweight LoRA adapters, each specialized on a distinct sub-domain
cluster of the target domain (clusters discovered via topic modeling or
metadata-driven splits). A small learned confidence gate is trained to produce,
for each input token/sequence: (a) a routing weight over the k adapters, and (b)
a scalar β ∈ [0,1] that mixes the adapter output with the base model's original
hidden state. When β is low, the model relies on base knowledge; when high,
injected knowledge dominates.

Gate architecture. A2-layer MLP over the hidden state of the last layer at the
final token position, outputting a softmax over adapters and a sigmoid-gated β.
Trained jointly with adapters via a regularized objective.

Training objective. Two terms:

• Domain accuracy — standard cross-entropy on domain data, but weighted by a
per-sample confidence bonus that down-weights examples the base model already
answers well (to focus injection on genuinely novel knowledge).
• General capability preservation — a distillation regularizer that penalizes
large β when the base model's output distribution on held-out general
benchmarks (MMLU subsets, GSM8K) has low entropy (high confidence),
preventing unnecessary overrides.

Inference. Single forward pass per token. Gating adds negligible latency (<1%
parameter overhead).

Dataset / Benchmark
We construct a multi-sub-domain biomedical benchmark from
public sources:

Sub-domain           Dataset                            Size         Source
Clinical guidelines  MedQA (subset)                     1.2K Q&A     USMLE
Pharmacology         DrugBank QA                        800 QA       DrugBank
Radiology reports    MIMIC-III (report impressions)     2K excerpts  PhysioNet
Molecular biology    PubMedQA                           1K QA        PubMed
General (probe)      MMLU (biomedical subset) +3        2.5K         MMLU
general sections

We also collect a training corpus by pooling the full source documents (not just
QA pairs) for each sub-domain, filtering for overlap with pre-training data to
remove ~90% intersection (document-level dedup against C4/RedPajama using
MinHash).

Evaluation Metrics| Category | Metric | Rationale |

|---|---|---| | Domain accuracy | Per sub-domain accuracy (F1/MCC for binary
tasks); macro-average | Measures injection effectiveness | | General retention |
Δ(MMLU_full), Δ(GSM8K) — absolute drop from pre-injection | Measures forgetting
| | Knowledge consistency | Counterfactual accuracy — same fact queried with3
phrasings, pass@1 agreement | Measures conflict robustness | | Sub-domain
interference | When querying sub-domain A, compute logit change on sub-domain B
adapters' outputs | Measures cross-talk | | Routing interpretability | Spearman
correlation between β and ground-truth fact novelty (was this fact in
pre-training?) | Validates gating works as intended |

2 Prompt-based injection — zero-shot with domain-relevant system prompt (no
parameter update).
3 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) — ColBERTv2 retriever over domain
corpus; top-3 chunks prepended to prompt.
4 Single LoRA — one rank-32 LoRA on all domain data.
5 Mixture of Adapters (fixed routing) — same k adapters, but routing weights
hard-coded by sub-domain label (oracle routing). Upper-bound measure.
6 Knowledge-editing baseline (MEMIT) — model editing at scale on the training
corpus.

Ablations1. No confidence gating — always mix with uniform β =0.5. Isolates the
benefit of adaptive routing.

2 No sub-domain clustering — single adapter with gating. Tests whether multiple
adapters matter.
3 No regularization term — train only on domain accuracy. Measures how much
general retention comes from the distillation regularizer vs. adapter
architecture alone.
4 Varying k —                                                                  Goodbye!

**1. Title**
Selective Neural Plasticity: Mitigating Semantic Entanglement in Domain-Specific Knowledge Injection via Gradient-Based Neuron Masking.

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with "knowledge injection" for specialized domains (e.g., clinical medicine, rare legal jurisdictions). Standard approaches like Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) or Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) frequently lead to two failures: (1) **Catastrophic Forgetting**, where the model loses general reasoning capabilities, and (2) **Semantic Entanglement**, where domain-specific terms are "overwritten" by general-purpose priors (e.g., a model interpreting a specific medical acronym through the lens of common internet slang). Current research often treats all model weights as equally available for update, but this ignores the fact that certain neurons are critical for "foundational logic" while others may be redundant or underutilized.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
The primary cause of hallucination and knowledge drift during domain injection is the corruption of "high-utility" general-reasoning neurons. I hypothesize that by identifying and freezing neurons with high Fisher Information relative to a general-purpose corpus, and restricting domain updates to "low-utility" neurons (Selective Neural Plasticity), we can inject specialized knowledge with 30% higher factual accuracy and significantly lower degradation of general reasoning compared to standard LoRA.

**4. Method**
The proposed method, **Selective Neural Plasticity (SNP)**, consists of three phases:
1.  **Importance Mapping:** Run a small, representative sample of a general dataset (e.g., TinyStories or C4) through the base model. Calculate the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) for all MLP (Multi-Layer Perceptron) weights to identify which neurons are most critical for general language modeling.
2.  **Sparsity Masking:** Create a binary mask $M$ that freezes the top $k\%$ of neurons (those with the highest FIM scores).
3.  **Targeted Injection:** Fine-tune the model on the domain-specific corpus using a modified objective function:
    $$\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{CE} + \lambda D_{KL}(P_{base} || P_{tuned})$$
    where the gradient updates are applied only to the non-masked (low-utility) neurons. This forces the model to "allocate" new knowledge into underutilized parameters rather than overwriting foundational ones.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **Injection Corpus:** *PubMed Central (PMC) Open Access Subset* (specifically focusing on rare diseases or recent pharmacology not present in the base model's pre-training cut-off).
*   **Evaluation Benchmarks:**
    *   *Domain-Specific:* **PubMedQA** and **BioASQ** (to test knowledge acquisition).
    *   *General Knowledge:* **MMLU** (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) to measure preservation of general reasoning.

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Knowledge Gain:** Delta in Accuracy on PubMedQA/BioASQ compared to the base model.
*   **Reasoning Retention:** The "Forgetting Score," defined as the percentage drop in MMLU performance post-injection.
*   **Hallucination Rate:** Human or LLM-as-a-judge evaluation of "Factuality" on 200 generated medical summaries.

**7. Baselines**
*   **Zero-Shot Base:** The un-tuned model (e.g., Llama-3-8B).
*   **Full Fine-Tuning (FFT):** Standard end-to-end training on the domain corpus.
*   **LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation):** The current industry standard for parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
*   **RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation):** Providing the domain knowledge in the prompt context without weight updates.

**8. Ablations**
*   **Random Masking:** Instead of using FIM, freeze a random $k\%$ of neurons to prove that the *selection* of neurons matters.
*   **Inverted Masking:** Freeze the "low-utility" neurons and train the "high-utility" ones (to demonstrate that this causes catastrophic failure).
*   **Sparsity Sensitivity:** Vary $k$ (the percentage of frozen neurons) from 10% to 90% to find the optimal balance between plasticity and stability.

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Dead Neurons:** If the base model is already highly compressed (e.g., a 1B parameter model), there may not be enough "low-utility" neurons to store complex new domain knowledge.
*   **Compute Overhead:** Calculating the Fisher Information Matrix for very large models (70B+) is computationally expensive, though this can be mitigated by using diagonal approximations or layer-wise estimation.
*   **Knowledge Complexity:** If the domain knowledge is fundamentally contradictory to the base model's world-view, the "low-utility" neurons might not be sufficient to override the primary logic paths.

**1. Title**
Contrastive Counterfactual Prompting (CCP): Enhancing Information Extraction through Synthetic Near-Miss Comparisons.

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Automated Information Extraction (IE) systems, particularly those based on Large Language Models (LLMs), frequently suffer from "semantic over-reliance." When a text contains entities that often appear together (e.g., "Elon Musk" and "Twitter"), the model may extract a relation (e.g., *Owner_Of*) based on internal prior knowledge rather than the specific linguistic evidence in the provided text. This leads to high recall but poor precision in "near-miss" scenarios—where the text describes a different or nuanced relationship (e.g., "Elon Musk criticized Twitter" vs. "Elon Musk bought Twitter"). Existing methods like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) focus on the *process* of extraction but do not force the model to distinguish the target relation from its semantic neighbors.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
Providing an LLM with a "minimally different" counterfactual version of the source text (where the relation is intentionally altered) alongside the original text will significantly improve extraction precision. Specifically, by forcing the model to explain why the original text satisfies a schema while the counterfactual does not, the model will better attend to discriminative syntactic markers it would otherwise ignore.

**4. Method**
The proposed method, **Contrastive Counterfactual Prompting (CCP)**, follows a three-stage pipeline:
1.  **Counterfactual Generation:** Given a source text $T$ and a candidate relation $R$, a secondary model (or a specific prompt) generates a "near-miss" text $T'$. $T'$ is identical to $T$ except for the specific verbs or connectors that define the relation (e.g., changing "acquired" to "is in talks to acquire").
2.  **Contrastive Prompting:** The extraction model is prompted with both $T$ and $T'$. The prompt asks: "In Text A, does Relation $R$ exist? In Text B, does Relation $R$ exist? Identify the specific words in Text A that make it different from Text B regarding this relation."
3.  **Final Extraction:** The model produces the structured output (triplet) based on the contrastive analysis performed in step 2.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **TACRED (Stanford):** A large-scale relation extraction dataset with 42 relation types.
*   **NYT-10:** For testing on distantly supervised data where noise is prevalent.
*   **Synthetic "Near-Miss" Set:** A curated subset of 500 examples where the text describes a relationship similar to, but not exactly matching, a target schema (e.g., *Per:Employee_of* vs. *Per:Founder_of*).

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Precision, Recall, and F1-score:** Standard IE metrics.
*   **False Positive Rate (FPR):** Specifically tracking if the model incorrectly extracts relations from "near-miss" distractors.
*   **Consistency Score:** Measuring if the model correctly identifies the relation in $T$ while correctly rejecting it in $T'$.

**7. Baselines**
*   **Zero-shot/Few-shot LLM (GPT-4/Llama-3):** Standard prompting without contrastive context.
*   **Chain-of-Thought (CoT):** Prompting the model to "think step-by-step" before extracting.
*   **Self-Correction:** Prompting the model to "review your previous answer for mistakes."

**8. Ablations**
*   **Random Distractor vs. Counterfactual:** Replacing the "near-miss" counterfactual with a random sentence from the dataset to see if the benefit comes from *any* additional context or specifically *contrastive* context.
*   **No-Explanation Contrast:** Providing $T$ and $T'$ but asking for the extraction directly without the "identify the difference" step.
*   **Gold vs. Synthetic Counterfactuals:** Comparing performance using human-written counterfactuals versus those generated by a smaller model (e.g., Mistral-7B).

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Hallucination in Generation:** The counterfactual generator might produce a text $T'$ that accidentally still satisfies the relation $R$, confusing the extraction model.

**1. Title**
Contrastive Counterfactual Prompting (CCP): Enhancing Information Extraction through Synthetic Near-Miss Comparisons.

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Automated Information Extraction (IE) systems, particularly those based on Large Language Models (LLMs), frequently suffer from "semantic over-reliance." When a text contains entities that often appear together (e.g., "Elon Musk" and "Twitter"), the model may extract a relation (e.g., *Owner_Of*) based on internal prior knowledge rather than the specific linguistic evidence in the provided text. This leads to high recall but poor precision in "near-miss" scenarios—where the text describes a different or nuanced relationship (e.g., "Elon Musk criticized Twitter" vs. "Elon Musk bought Twitter"). Existing methods like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) focus on the *process* of extraction but do not force the model to distinguish the target relation from its semantic neighbors.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
Providing an LLM with a "minimally different" counterfactual version of the source text (where the relation is intentionally altered) alongside the original text will significantly improve extraction precision. Specifically, by forcing the model to explain why the original text satisfies a schema while the counterfactual does not, the model will better attend to discriminative syntactic markers it would otherwise ignore.

**4. Method**
The proposed method, **Contrastive Counterfactual Prompting (CCP)**, follows a three-stage pipeline:
1.  **Counterfactual Generation:** Given a source text $T$ and a candidate relation $R$, a secondary model (or a specific prompt) generates a "near-miss" text $T'$. $T'$ is identical to $T$ except for the specific verbs or connectors that define the relation (e.g., changing "acquired" to "is in talks to acquire").
2.  **Contrastive Prompting:** The extraction model is prompted with both $T$ and $T'$. The prompt asks: "In Text A, does Relation $R$ exist? In Text B, does Relation $R$ exist? Identify the specific words in Text A that make it different from Text B regarding this relation."
3.  **Final Extraction:** The model produces the structured output (triplet) based on the contrastive analysis performed in step 2.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **TACRED (Stanford):** A large-scale relation extraction dataset with 42 relation types.
*   **NYT-10:** For testing on distantly supervised data where noise is prevalent.
*   **Synthetic "Near-Miss" Set:** A curated subset of 500 examples where the text describes a relationship similar to, but not exactly matching, a target schema (e.g., *Per:Employee_of* vs. *Per:Founder_of*).

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Precision, Recall, and F1-score:** Standard IE metrics.
*   **False Positive Rate (FPR):** Specifically tracking if the model incorrectly extracts relations from "near-miss" distractors.
*   **Consistency Score:** Measuring if the model correctly identifies the relation in $T$ while correctly rejecting it in $T'$.

**7. Baselines**
*   **Zero-shot/Few-shot LLM (GPT-4/Llama-3):** Standard prompting without contrastive context.
*   **Chain-of-Thought (CoT):** Prompting the model to "think step-by-step" before extracting.
*   **Self-Correction:** Prompting the model to "review your previous answer for mistakes."

**8. Ablations**
*   **Random Distractor vs. Counterfactual:** Replacing the "near-miss" counterfactual with a random sentence from the dataset to see if the benefit comes from *any* additional context or specifically *contrastive* context.
*   **No-Explanation Contrast:** Providing $T$ and $T'$ but asking for the extraction directly without the "identify the difference" step.
*   **Gold vs. Synthetic Counterfactuals:** Comparing performance using human-written counterfactuals versus those generated by a smaller model (e.g., Mistral-7B).

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Hallucination in Generation:** The counterfactual generator might produce a text $T'$ that accidentally still satisfies the relation $R$, confusing the extraction model.
*   **Token Overhead:** CCP doubles the number of tokens per prompt, increasing latency and API costs.
*   **Feasibility:** High. LLMs are already adept at "text editing" tasks; using one to generate a counterfactual for another is a standard multi-agent pattern. The primary risk is ensuring the "near-miss" is subtle enough to be useful but not so ambiguous that it becomes a subjective labeling task.

### 1. Title
**Cognitive Calibration: Evaluating LLM UX through Real-time Uncertainty Visualization.**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Current Large Language Model (LLM) evaluations focus heavily on model performance (accuracy, reasoning, safety) rather than the human-AI interaction loop. A primary pain point in LLM UX is the "Black Box" phenomenon: users cannot distinguish between a model’s high-confidence factual statement and a high-confidence hallucination. This leads to "Ghost Chasing," where users spend excessive time iteratively prompting a model that lacks the underlying data to answer correctly. Improving UX requires moving beyond raw accuracy to "Cognitive Calibration"—the degree to which a user’s trust in the model matches the model’s actual competence at a specific moment.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
Explicitly visualizing token-level uncertainty (e.g., via confidence heatmaps) in the UI significantly reduces task completion time and "Prompt Iteration Fatigue" compared to using a more accurate but opaque model. Specifically, a user will be more productive with a 7B-parameter model that highlights its own uncertainty than with a 70B-parameter model that presents all outputs with uniform visual certainty.

### 4. Method
The study employs a 2x2 factorial design with a controlled user experiment:
1.  **Participants:** 60 users (30 technical, 30 non-technical) tasked with solving complex information retrieval and code debugging problems.
2.  **Interface Variables:**
    *   *Control:* Standard chat interface (plain text).
    *   *Experimental:* "Uncertainty UI" where text background color maps to log-probability (e.g., white = high confidence, deep red = low confidence/high entropy).
3.  **Model Variables:**
    *   *High-Capability (HC):* A SOTA model (e.g., GPT-4o).
    *   *Mid-Capability (MC):* A smaller, more error-prone model (e.g., Llama-3-8B).
4.  **Task Design:** Users are given "Impossible Tasks" (questions with no answer in the training data) and "Difficult Tasks" (requiring multi-step reasoning).
5.  **Procedure:** Users are timed as they attempt to reach a "verified" answer. We track how quickly they give up on impossible tasks and how efficiently they verify difficult ones.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **Tasks:** A curated subset of the **StrategyQA** and **HaluEval** datasets, modified to include "Unanswerable" variants.
*   **Ground Truth:** Each task has a verified "Correct" or "Unanswerable" status.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Calibration Score (Primary):** The correlation between the user's reported confidence in an answer and the model's actual correctness.
*   **Time-to-Abandon (TTA):** Time spent on unanswerable tasks (lower is better, indicating the user recognized the model’s limitations quickly).
*   **Prompt Iteration Count:** The number of follow-up prompts required to reach a correct conclusion.
*   **System Usability Scale (SUS):** Post-task subjective satisfaction.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Baseline 1 (Standard HC):** GPT-4o with no uncertainty visualization.
*   **Baseline 2 (Verbalized Uncertainty):** A model prompted to explicitly state "I am unsure" in the text response (e.g., "Self-Correction" or "Chain-of-Verification" methods).

### 8. Ablations
*   **Granularity Ablation:** Compare token-level heatmaps vs. sentence-level confidence scores.
*   **Modality Ablation:** Compare visual heatmaps vs. numerical percentages (e.g., "85% confident") displayed at the end of the response.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Cognitive Overload:** Users may find flickering colors or heatmaps distracting, leading to lower performance despite better information.
*   **The "Hallucination Trap":** LLMs are often "confidently wrong." If the model assigns high log-probability to a hallucination, the UI will mislead the user. This experiment assumes a non-zero correlation between log-probs and truthfulness, which is a known limitation in RLHF-tuned models.
*   **Feasibility:** Accessing log-probabilities is easy for open-source models (Llama/Mistral) but restricted for some closed-source APIs, potentially limiting the choice of "High-Capability" models.

This approach is computationally expensive and inefficient because many prompts are either too easy (all models pass) or too hard (all models fail), providing little information about the relative performance of models. As the number of models and benchmarks grows, the cost of maintaining high-fidelity rankings becomes a bottleneck for open-source research.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
Evaluating LLMs on a subset of prompts selected via an active **Item Response Theory (IRT)** framework—specifically choosing prompts with high "discrimination" parameters for models of a specific "ability" level—can achieve a ranking correlation (Spearman’s $\rho > 0.95$) with the full benchmark while using less than 20% of the total inference budget.

**Why this is surprising:** Most researchers treat benchmarks as monolithic sets. This hypothesis suggests that for any given pair of models, the vast majority of benchmark questions are "noise" that does not contribute to their relative ranking, and that these informative questions can be identified on-the-fly without prior knowledge of the new model’s specific weights.

### 4. Method
The proposed method, **Active-IRT**, treats LLM evaluation as an adaptive testing problem:
1.  **Calibration Phase:** Using a set of "anchor" models (e.g., Llama-2, GPT-3.5, Mistral-7B), estimate the parameters for every prompt in a large pool (e.g., MMLU) using a 2-Parameter Logistic (2PL) IRT model. Each prompt is assigned a *difficulty* ($\beta$) and a *discrimination* ($\alpha$).
2.  **Estimation Loop:** When a new model $M$ is evaluated:
    *   Start with a small random seed of 10 prompts to get an initial "ability" ($\theta$) estimate.
    *   **Active Selection:** Select the next $N$ prompts that maximize the **Fisher Information** at the current estimated $\theta$. This prioritizes prompts where the model has a ~50% chance of success and the prompt is known to distinguish well between similar models.
    *   **Update:** Re-estimate $\theta$ using Maximum Likelihood Estimation.
3.  **Termination:** Stop when the standard error of $\theta$ falls below a predefined threshold.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **Primary Pool:** The **MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding)** dataset (57 subjects, ~16k questions).
*   **Secondary Pool:** **GSM8K** (for math-specific ranking) to test if the IRT parameters generalize across reasoning tasks.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Ranking Fidelity:** Spearman’s Rank Correlation ($\rho$) between the Active-IRT leaderboard and the "Gold Standard" leaderboard (full benchmark results).
*   **Efficiency Gain:** The ratio of prompts used in Active-IRT vs. the full benchmark to reach the same ranking stability.
*   **Stability:** The variance in a model's rank when the active selection is repeated with different random seeds.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Uniform Random Sampling:** Selecting a fixed percentage of prompts randomly from the benchmark.
*   **Static Difficulty Pruning:** Using only "hard" questions (as determined by average accuracy across anchor models) for all evaluations.
*   **Full Benchmark:** The standard approach of running every model on every prompt.

### 8. Ablations
*   **Anchor Set Size:** How many models are needed in the calibration phase to get reliable prompt parameters? (Test with 3, 5, 10, and 20 anchors).
*   **IRT Model Complexity:** Compare the 1PL (Rasch) model (difficulty only) against the 2PL model (difficulty + discrimination).
*   **Cross-Domain Transfer:** Use IRT parameters calibrated on "Humanities" prompts to evaluate models on "STEM" prompts to test parameter robustness.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Model Overfitting:** If a model is trained specifically on the "high discrimination" prompts, the leaderboard becomes gameable. (Mitigation: Keep the IRT parameters and selected subsets private or rotate them).
*   **Parameter Drift:** As models get significantly smarter, prompts that were once discriminative may become "too easy" for all new models (ceiling effect). (Mitigation: Periodically update the anchor set with state-of-the-art models).
*   **Computational Overhead:** The cost of re-estimating $\theta$ after every few prompts must be lower than the cost of the LLM inference itself. (Mitigation: Batch the active selection process).

Research Proposal: Evaluating Context-Appropriate Diversity in Neural Text
Generation## Title
CoDE: A Context-Dependent Diversity Evaluation Framework for
Open-Ended Text Generation

Problem
Existing diversity metrics for text generation (Distinct-n, Self-BLEU,
Entropy-5, TTR) all share a fundamental flaw: they measure diversity as a single
scalar aggregated over a corpus, independent of the input context. This means:

• A model that generates the same generic response to every prompt can score
high on diversity if responses differ across prompts (high inter-prompt
diversity) while being pathologically repetitive within each response (low
intra-prompt diversity).
• A factual QA model that should produce low-variance answers is punished for
being "not diverse."
• There is no established way to distinguish appropriate diversity (multiple
valid paraphrases of the same meaning) from inappropriate diversity
(hallucinated facts or topic drift).

The central gap is that diversity is not a single target to maximize—it is a
distributional property that should match the conditional distribution implied
by the input.

Hypothesis
Diversity in text generation can be decomposed into two orthogonal
components—intra-response diversity (variety within a single generated text) and
inter-response diversity (variety across generations for the same input, i.e.,
model stochasticity)—and each has a context-dependent expected range that can be
estimated from the training data or human references. A model whose diversity
falls outside this expected range (too high or too low) is exhibiting a failure
mode that existing aggregate metrics miss.

Method
CoDE (Context-Dependent Diversity Evaluation) proceeds in three stages:

1 Reference-conditional diversity calibration. For each input context in the
evaluation set, collect a set of human-written references (≥5 per context).
Compute per-context diversity statistics on the references to establish an
expected diversity interval per context and per diversity facet. Facets
include:

• Lexical diversity: Distinct-1, Distinct-2, corrected TTR (Herdan's TTR)
• Structural diversity: syntactic tree depth variance, POS tag entropy -
Semantic diversity: pairwise sentence-BERT cosine variance among candidate
generations for the same prompt2. Within-vs-across response decomposition.
For each model under evaluation, generate K responses per prompt (K ≥10).
Compute:
• Intra-response diversity: averaged per-response metrics (e.g., average
Self-BLEU of a response against itself in sliding windows)
• Inter-response diversity: diversity across the K generations for the same
prompt (e.g., pairwise BERTScore variance, corpus-level Distinct-n across
generations)

3 Deviation scoring. For each (model, prompt, facet) triple, measure the signed
deviation of the model's diversity from the human-established interval:

• Deviation ∈ [−1, +1] where negative = under-diverse (more repetitive than
humans), positive = over-diverse (more varied than humans, potentially
hallucinatory)
• Aggregate: mean absolute deviation across facets = CoDE score (lower is
better)

Dataset / Benchmark
Construct a multi-domain diversity benchmark spanning
contexts with intrinsically different diversity expectations:

Domain                    Expected diversity        Rationale
Factoid QA (SQuAD2.0,     Low inter + low intra     One correct answer, short
TriviaQA)
Story generation          High intra, moderate      One narrative, varied
(WritingPrompts,          inter                     style
ROCStories)
Data-to-text (WebNLG,     Low intra, moderate       Fixed facts, varied
E2E NLG)                  inter                     surface form
Open-ended dialogue       High intra + high inter   Many valid turns
(PersonaChat,
DailyDialog)
Creative continuation     High intra + high inter   Many valid completions
(Story Cloze, CommonGen)

Sample500 prompts per domain (2,500 total) with ≥5 human references each.

Evaluation Metrics1. Primary metric: CoDE score (mean absolute deviation from
the human diversity interval across all facets and domains).

2 Secondary metrics: Breakdown by facet (lexical, structural, semantic) and by
domain.
3 Validation metric: Correlation with human judgment of "appropriate diversity"
(Likert1–5) on a held-out set of200 (model, prompt, response) triples rated
by ≥3 annotators. Target: Spearman ρ ≥0.6 against the CoDE score.

Baselines| Baseline | What it measures | Expected limitation |

|---|---|---| | Distinct-1 / Distinct-2 | Surface n-gram novelty | No context
conditioning, length-biased | | Self-BLEU | Intra-corpus n-gram overlap | Single
scalar, no per-context or per-facet breakdown | | Entropy-5 / Entropy-n | n-gram
distribution uniformity | Ignores semantic and structural diversity | | Zipf
coefficient | Frequency-rank distribution fit | Only describes the tail;
insensitive to local repetition | | vMeasure (Hashimoto et al.,2019) |
Cluster-conditional diversity | Requires latent cluster assignments; not
natively context-conditional | | MAUVE (Pillutla et al.,2021) | Divergence
between model and human output distributions | Measures distribution matching,
not per-response diversity |

Ablations1. Reference-count ablation: Vary the number of human references per
prompt from1 to20. Hypothesis: the CoDE score stabilizes at ≥5 references.

2 Facet ablation: Remove each facet one at a time and measure correlation drop
with human judgment. Identifies which facet contributes most signal.
3 Pooling ablation: Replace per-prompt intervals with corpus-level intervals
(the current default in the field). Hypothesis: the per-prompt decomposition
is the main source of improvement.
4 Generation count ablation: Vary K (number of generations per prompt) from2
to50. Identifies the minimum K for stable inter-response estimates.
5 Metric-level baselines: Replace the deviation formulation with a simple
average of existing metrics conditioned on nothing. Measures the marginal
gain of context-conditional calibration.

Expected Failure Modes1. Reference quality collapse. If human references are
themselves low-quality or inconsistently diverse (e.g., crowd workers producing
minimal-effort responses), the "expected interval" becomes meaningless.
Mitigation: filter references via an automatic quality check (e.g., minimum
length, minimum Distinct-1 >0) and exclude outlying prompts where
inter-reference variance is >2σ from the domain mean.

2 Metric saturation on long-form generation. For very long generations (stories
>500 tokens), intra-response lexical diversity may saturate (all models
approach the same high Distinct-n), making the lexical facet uninformative.
Mitigation: use sliding-window diversity (window =100 tokens) and report the
minimum window diversity, not the aggregate, to capture local repetition that
longer texts hide.
3 Semantic diversity metric conflates quality with diversity. Sentence-BERT
variance could be high simply because generations are incoherent rather than
genuinely diverse. Mitigation: compute semantic diversity only over
generations that pass a minimum fluency/coherence threshold (e.g., perplexity
< a domain-specific cutoff). Flag the model's quality-diversity trade-off
explicitly as a secondary diagnostic.
4 Domain boundary ambiguity. The "expected diversity" for an ambiguous prompt
(e.g., a news headline that could be either factual or editorial) may not
fall cleanly into one domain bin. Mitigation: report per-prompt deviations
rather than only domain aggregates, and provide prompt-level visualization
for outlier analysis.
5 Inter-response diversity is confounded by sampling temperature. A model run
at temperature1.0 will naturally produce more inter-response variation than
at temperature0.1. The CoDE score must hold sampling hyperparameters fixed
across all models, or the benchmark becomes a comparison of sampling
strategies rather than model architectures. Mitigation: standardize to
temperature =0.7, top-p =0.9 for all models, and include a sensitivity
experiment reporting how CoDE changes with temperature.

### 1. Title
**Structural vs. Lexical Diversity: Quantifying Logical Trajectory Variety in Chain-of-Thought Generation**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Current evaluation metrics for diversity in text generation—such as Self-BLEU, Distinct-n, and semantic embedding variance—primarily focus on surface-level lexical variation or broad semantic shifts. However, in the context of Large Language Models (LLMs) performing reasoning tasks (e.g., Chain-of-Thought), these metrics fail to distinguish between "useful diversity" (exploring different logical paths to a solution) and "noise" (mere synonym swapping or stylistic jitter). Consequently, models that appear "diverse" by standard metrics may simply be generating redundant reasoning steps in different words, which does not improve ensemble techniques like Self-Consistency.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
Increasing lexical diversity (vocabulary and syntax variance) beyond a certain threshold in multi-step reasoning tasks is negatively correlated with reasoning accuracy, whereas increasing **Structural Diversity**—defined as the variety of unique logical dependency graphs extracted from reasoning chains—is positively correlated with the performance gain of majority-vote ensembles.

### 4. Method
The proposed method involves three stages:
1.  **Generation:** Sample $k$ reasoning paths (Chain-of-Thought) for a given prompt using high-temperature sampling or diverse beam search.
2.  **Structural Extraction:** Use a smaller, frozen "Extractor" model (e.g., GPT-4o-mini or a fine-tuned Llama-3) to convert each reasoning path into a simplified **Reasoning Graph**. Nodes represent intermediate propositions or calculations, and edges represent logical dependencies (e.g., "Step A implies Step B").
3.  **Diversity Quantification:**
    *   Calculate **Structural Entropy**: The Shannon entropy of the set of unique graph isomorphisms generated across $k$ samples.
    *   Calculate **Mean Graph Edit Distance (mGED)**: The average distance between the extracted logical structures.
4.  **Correlation Analysis:** Measure how these structural metrics correlate with the accuracy of a Self-Consistency ensemble compared to traditional metrics like Self-BLEU.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **GSM8K (Grade School Math):** To evaluate structural diversity in deterministic mathematical logic.
*   **StrategyQA:** To evaluate diversity in multi-hop commonsense reasoning where multiple evidence paths might exist.
*   **Big-Bench Hard (BBH):** Specifically the "Logical Deduction" and "Formal Fallacies" subsets.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Structural Entropy (Proposed):** Diversity based on unique logical paths.
*   **Self-Consistency Gain:** The delta between the accuracy of a single greedy sample and a majority vote of $k$ diverse samples.
*   **Standard Diversity Baselines:** Self-BLEU (overlap), Distinct-n (n-gram variety), and V-Measure (cluster quality in embedding space).

### 7. Baselines
*   **Temperature Sampling ($T=0.7$ to $1.2$):** The standard method for inducing diversity.
*   **Diverse Beam Search (DBS):** A decoding-time intervention to force lexical variety.
*   **Stochastic Paraphrasing:** A baseline where a model is explicitly prompted to "rephrase the previous reasoning path" to see if lexical diversity without structural change improves results.

### 8. Ablations
*   **Granularity of Extraction:** Compare "Sentence-level" nodes vs. "Proposition-level" nodes in the reasoning graph.
*   **Model Size for Extraction:** Testing if a 7B model can extract logical structures as reliably as a 70B model for the purpose of the metric.
*   **Graph vs. Sequence:** Comparing the graph-based diversity to a simple "step-ordering" diversity (treating the logic as a linear sequence of abstract tags).

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Extraction Noise:** The "Extractor" model might fail to capture the true logic, or it might hallucinate dependencies, leading to an inaccurate Structural Entropy score.
*   **Isomorphism Complexity:** Computing graph isomorphisms for very long reasoning chains (e.g., 20+ steps) could become computationally expensive, though this can be mitigated by simplifying the graph schema.
*   **Redundancy in Logic:** In simple tasks (like basic arithmetic), there may only be one valid logical path, making the structural diversity metric collapse to zero regardless of lexical variety. This makes the metric more suitable for complex, multi-hop reasoning than for simple tasks.

not per-response diversity |

Ablations1. Reference-count ablation: Vary the number of human references per

is the main source of improvement.

approach the same high Distinct-n), making the lexical facet uninformative.

Research Proposal: Robust AI-Generated Content Detection via
Adversarially-Calibrated Uncertainty Estimation (R-ACE)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Title
R-ACE: Reducing False Positives in AI-Generated Content Detection through
Uncertainty-Aware Calibration and Adversarial Human Text

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current AI-generated text detectors (e.g., GPTZero, OpenAI Classifier,
DetectGPT, Fast-DetectGPT) achieve high accuracy on held-out test sets, but
suffer from asymmetric error rates: false positive rates (FPR) of5–30% on
human-written text, especially text that is factual, formulaic, or edited by
non-native speakers. This makes them unreliable for high-stakes deployment
(academic integrity, content moderation, misinformation tracking). The core
problem is that detectors are calibrated on machine vs. human distinctions from
static benchmarks but fail under distribution shift toward the "hard decision
boundary" — text that is highly structured, low-perplexity, or edited to mimic
machine output.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
False positives arise because detectors conflate "low perplexity /
high predictability" with "machine-origin." Human-written text with low
token-level surprisal (technical writing, legal text, edited prose) occupies the
same region of the detector's latent space as AI-generated text.

Specifically: Training an AI-content detector with an explicit uncertainty head
and calibrating it on a stratified mix of naturally-occurring human text and
adversarially-perturbed human text (designed to mimic AI output patterns) will
reduce FPR@95%TPR by at least40% relative to the current state of the art,
without degrading true positive rate on genuine AI text.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
We propose a three-component architecture:

1 Base feature extractor: A frozen pre-trained LLM (e.g., Llama-3-8B) that
computes per-token log-likelihoods and hidden state representations — the
same backbone used by Fast-DetectGPT.
2 Uncertainty-aware detection head: Instead of a deterministic classifier,
train a deep evidential regression head (Amini et al.,2020) that outputs both
a machine-likelihood score and an epistemic uncertainty estimate. This
enables the model to abstain or down-weight predictions on inputs far from
the training distribution.
3 Adversarial human text augmentation: Construct a calibration dataset by
taking human-written text (from domains known to trigger false positives —
see Dataset) and applying minimal edits that push it toward the machine-text
region:

• Reduce token-level perplexity via greedy truncation of rare tokens - Insert
formulaic transition phrases common in LLM output - Apply "LLM-rewriting"
(GPT-4o-mini instructed to preserve meaning but "make this text look more
like it was written by an AI")

This creates a controlled set of near-boundary negative examples.

Inference procedure: Given input text, compute the machine-likelihood score with
uncertainty interval. Flag as AI-generated only if (a) the score exceeds the
decision threshold and (b) the epistemic uncertainty is below a second
threshold. Otherwise, classify as "uncertain / likely human."

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Split | Source | Size (docs) |

|-------|--------|-------------| | Train: human | C4 (filtered), Wikipedia,
legal contracts, arXiv papers |50,000 | | Train: AI | Machine-Generated Text
(MGT) from GPT-4o, Llama-3, Claude-3.5 |50,000 | | Calibration: adversarial
human | Human text from above + adversarial edits (Per-Method) |10,000 | | Test:
standard | HC3, M4, RAID (held-out) — balanced human/AI |10,000 | | Test: hard
FPR set | Human-written: non-native English essays (TOEFL corpus), PubMed
abstracts, SEC filings, Wikipedia stubs |5,000 |

Key benchmark addition: The "hard FPR set" deliberately collects domains where
current detectors fail. We will release this as a public stress-test suite.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics1. Primary: False Positive Rate at95% True Positive Rate
(FPR@95%TPR) — measures false alarms at a fixed recall level2. Secondary: Area
Under ROC Curve (AUROC), Area Under Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC)

3 Calibration: Expected Calibration Error (ECE) on the machine-likelihood
score, separately computed for human and AI subsets4. Abstention quality:
Fraction of human text flagged as "uncertain" (target: ≤5% on standard test,
≤15% on hard FPR set)
4 Robustness: Performance under domain shift (evaluate on held-out domains not
seen in training)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Key Idea |

|----------|----------| | DetectGPT (Mitchell et al.,2023) | Curvature-based
detection via perturbation | | Fast-DetectGPT (Bao et al.,2024) | Conditional
probability curvature (faster variant) | | Ghostbuster (Verma et al.,2024) |
Feature-based classifier on perturbed texts | | Binoculars (Hans et al.,2024) |
Cross-model perplexity ratio | | OpenAI AI Classifier (2023) | Fine-tuned
RoBERTa (retrospective; API-based) | | DeepEvidential baseline | Same
architecture as ours without adversarial human augmentation |

All baselines are re-run on our evaluation suite with their published
hyperparameters.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations| Ablation | What it tests |

|----------|---------------| | No uncertainty head | Deterministic classifier
only → value of the evidential component | | No adversarial augmentation | Train
only on natural human/AI splits → value of hard negatives | | Perplexity-only
threshold | Replace learned classifier with a p(x) cutoff → value of learned
features | | Single-threshold inference | Remove the uncertainty-based
abstention rule → value of two-threshold inference | | Different base LLM | Swap
Llama-3-8B for GPT-NeoX-20B → sensitivity to backbone |

Each ablation is evaluated on the same metrics above.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Domain mismatch still dominates: The hard FPR set may
still be too broad. If adversarial augmentation only covers specific failure
modes, FPR may improve on the calibration domains but not generalize to unseen
low-perplexity domains (e.g., poetry, legal boilerplate from a jurisdiction not
in training).

2 Uncertainty head over-abstains: The epistemic uncertainty threshold may be
too conservative, flagging many genuine AI texts as "uncertain" and reducing
the usable detection rate. This creates a precision/coverage tradeoff that
deployment may reject.
3 Adversarial edits create detectable artifacts: The procedure for generating
adversarial human text may introduce n-gram or stylistic artifacts
(repetition patterns, specific transition phrases) that the classifier learns
as spurious features, causing it to fail on unmodified human text from the
same domains.
4 Calibration gap: Evidential regression on text may produce poorly calibrated
uncertainties due to the high-dimensional, non-i.i.d. nature of the input
distribution. The uncertainty estimates may not reflect true epistemic
uncertainty, just variations in training density.
5 Computational cost: The two-threshold inference and deep evidential head add
~2× inference overhead vs. Fast-DetectGPT, which may be prohibitive for
real-time detection at scale.
6 Adversarial human text boundaries are unclear: There is no principled way to
define "how much editing makes human text look like AI text." The boundary is
inherently continuous, and the augmentation procedure may be hard to
reproduce across labs.
