Research Proposal: Structured Memory Banks for Long-Context Grounding in LLMs##
Title
Memory-Augmented Hierarchical Summarization (MAHS): Improving Long-Context
Grounding Without Full Attention Retraining

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Large Language Models suffer from the lost-in-the-middle problem — when
prompted with documents exceeding ~8K tokens, accuracy on facts located in the
middle of the context degrades sharply, even for models that claim128K+ context
windows. Two root causes: (1) softmax attention dilutes signal across many
tokens, and (2) positional encodings (RoPE, ALiBi) lose relative resolution at
extreme lengths. Existing solutions (ring attention, sparse attention,
state-space models) either require expensive full retraining or sacrifice recall
on mid-context facts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Injecting a separately trained, retrieval-augmented memory bank —
built from hierarchically compressed chunks of the input context — into the
LLM's cross-attention layers will recover mid-context fact recall to within90%
of short-context performance without fine-tuning the base LLM. The memory bank
acts as a "second path" that bypasses diluted full-context attention.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
Component1 — Hierarchical Chunking & Summarization

• Split the input context into fixed-size chunks (e.g.,512 tokens each).
• For each chunk, generate a short natural-language summary (<=64 tokens) using
a lightweight LM (e.g., Phi-3-mini). This forms the first summary layer.
• Recursively apply the same process to the summary sequence to produce a
second, coarser summary layer.
• Store all chunks and summaries in a flat key-value store keyed by chunk
position and semantic embedding.

Component2 — Retrieval-Augmented Memory Attention

• Insert a small set of memory tokens (e.g.,128) at the start of each attention
layer's key-value cache during generation.
• At each decoding step, retrieve the top-k chunks/summaries (by cosine
similarity to the current hidden state) from the memory bank.
• Encode the retrieved chunks as additional key-value pairs appended to the
existing full-context KV cache for that layer, but with a separate learned
gating scalar that down-weights the full-context path when memory retrieval
has high confidence.

Component3 — Training (Lightweight)

• Freeze the base LLM entirely.
• Train only the memory encoder (a small transformer, ~50M params), the
retrieval projection layer, and the gating scalars.
• Training objective: next-token prediction on long-document perplexity, with
an auxiliary contrastive loss that pulls the hidden state closer to the
embedding of the chunk containing the ground-truth next token.

Base model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (128K context)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Benchmark | Purpose | Metric |

|-----------|---------|--------| | RULER (Hsieh et al.,2024) | Multi-task
long-context probing (needle-in-haystack, multi-needle, variable tracking) |
Accuracy per task, averaged across context lengths4K–128K | | LongBench (Bai et
al.,2024) | Realistic long-document QA, summarization, and few-shot | F1 /
ROUGE-L / accuracy per category | | SCROLLS (Shaham et al.,2022) | Long
narrative & legal document QA | F1 | | Custom: Mid-Context Perturbation Set | A
constructed50K-token corpus where every question's answer appears only in the
middle third (positions33%–66%) | F1 gap relative to same question with answer
in first10% |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics1. Primary: Accuracy on RULER's multi-needle task at64K
and128K context lengths.

2 Secondary:

• Perplexity on held-out long documents (16K–128K).
• Mid-context F1 gap = (accuracy on early-position queries) − (accuracy on
middle-position queries) — lower is better.
• Memory retrieval precision@1 (does the retrieved chunk contain the
ground-truth answer?).

3 Efficiency: Wall-clock time per generation token vs. baseline Llama-3.1 full
attention.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Why |

|----------|-----| | Base Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (full attention,128K) |
Reference point for lost-in-the-middle | | Llama-3.1 with chunked
cross-attention (no memory, no retrieval) | Ablates the retrieval component | |
LongLoRA fine-tune on long documents | Ablates the "no fine-tuning" claim | |
InfLLM (sparse attention + retrieval) | Closest published method; shows whether
memory bank approach improves over retrieval-only | | GraphRAG / MemWalker
(summarize-then-retrieve) | Tests whether hierarchical summarization alone
(without retrieval gating) is sufficient |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. No hierarchical summaries — flat chunk retrieval only. Tests whether
the summary hierarchy matters.

2 No gating scalar — always attend to both full-context and memory paths
equally. Tests whether the learned down-weighting is essential.
3 Memory bank size sweep —32,64,128,256 memory tokens. Characterizes the
trade-off between compute overhead and recall.
4 k retrieval sweep — top-1, top-3, top-5 chunks retrieved. Tests sensitivity
to retrieval depth.
5 Base model size — repeat best configuration on Llama-3.1-70B to test scaling
behavior.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation in Proposal |

|---|---| | Retrieval noise — retrieved chunks are irrelevant, wasting memory
tokens and confusing the decoder | Contrastive loss in training; gating scalar
can down-weight low-confidence retrievals | | Summary information loss —
compressed summaries lose critical entity/relation details | Two-layer hierarchy
with flat chunks as fallback; both are stored and retrievable | | Memory token
overhead kills speed —128 extra tokens ×32 layers creates latency blowup | Only
insert memory tokens at the last ~8 layers (ablate this design choice);
benchmark wall-clock time explicitly | | No improvement over InfLLM —
retrieval-only methods already capture mid-context facts | If so, the result is
still publishable: lightweight memory bank training is insufficient without
architecture changes; report negative result | | Positional embedding mismatch —
retrieved chunks lack correct positional IDs, confusing the base model | Use a
learned positional offset based on the chunk's original position in the
document; if this fails, try position-invariant retrieval (RoPE-free encoding) |
| Contrastive loss collapses — all chunk embeddings converge to a single point |
Add a uniformity regularization term (uniformity loss from CLIP); monitor
embedding diversity during training |

### 1. Title
**Dynamic Bottleneck Anchoring (DBA): Enhancing Long-Context Retrieval via Sparse Hierarchical Latent Tokens**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Current Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with "attention dilution" and the "lost-in-the-middle" phenomenon. As context windows expand to hundreds of thousands of tokens, the softmax attention mechanism distributes probability mass across a vast number of keys, often causing the model to miss fine-grained details or fail to synthesize information across distant segments. While linear attention and State Space Models (SSMs) address computational complexity, they often sacrifice the high-fidelity retrieval capabilities of standard Transformers. There is a need for a mechanism that maintains the precision of full attention while providing a structured "map" of the context to prevent signal degradation.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
Restricting long-range attention to a set of periodically placed "Anchor Tokens"—which are forced to compress local context into a dense latent representation—will improve long-context retrieval accuracy. This is surprising because it suggests that **bottlenecking** information (intentionally losing raw token data in favor of synthesized anchors) will yield higher retrieval performance than allowing the model to attend to the entire raw token stream.

### 4. Method
The proposed method, **Dynamic Bottleneck Anchoring (DBA)**, involves the following:
1.  **Anchor Insertion:** During fine-tuning, a special trainable token `[ANC]` is inserted every $k$ tokens (e.g., $k=512$).
2.  **Hierarchical Attention Masking:**
    *   Standard tokens in a block attend to each other (local attention).
    *   Standard tokens are *not* allowed to attend to distant standard tokens.
    *   Standard tokens *are* allowed to attend to all preceding `[ANC]` tokens.
    *   `[ANC]` tokens attend to all previous `[ANC]` tokens and the $k$ raw tokens in their immediate local block.
3.  **Compression Objective:** To ensure `[ANC]` tokens capture meaningful data, a secondary objective is added during training where the model must reconstruct a randomly masked keyword from the local block using only the `[ANC]` token representation.
4.  **Inference:** At inference time, the KV-cache for raw tokens can be evicted for distant blocks, keeping only the KV-pairs for `[ANC]` tokens, significantly reducing memory overhead while maintaining a "global map" of the document.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **Needle In A Haystack (NIAH):** To test basic retrieval at varying depths and context lengths (up to 128k).
*   **LongBench:** To evaluate performance on real-world tasks like multi-document summarization and long-form QA.
*   **RULER:** A more complex benchmark that tests variable-count retrieval and frequent item extraction to ensure the anchors aren't just capturing the "gist" but also specific entities.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Recall Accuracy:** Percentage of correct "needle" retrievals in NIAH.
*   **F1 Score / Rough-L:** For summarization and QA tasks in LongBench.
*   **Perplexity vs. Context Length:** To ensure the model remains stable as the sequence grows.
*   **KV-Cache Compression Ratio:** Measurement of memory savings compared to full-attention models.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Standard Transformer (Full Attention):** To establish the "lost-in-the-middle" baseline.
*   **LongLoRA / YaRN:** Current state-of-the-art methods for extending context windows via RoPE scaling.
*   **StreamingLLM:** To compare against sliding-window attention mechanisms that use "attention sinks."
*   **Mamba / Jamba:** To compare against hybrid SSM-Transformer architectures.

### 8. Ablations
*   **Anchor Density:** Testing performance with $k=128, 256, 512, 1024$ to find the optimal compression ratio.
*   **Without Compression Objective:** Training the anchors without the reconstruction loss to see if the attention mechanism alone is sufficient to learn useful latent representations.
*   **Anchor-Only Attention:** Forcing the model to *only* look at anchors (no local attention) to test the limits of the latent representation.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Information Smearing:** The `[ANC]` tokens might aggregate information too broadly, losing specific numerical data or names (loss of granularity).
*   **Training Divergence:** Introducing a secondary reconstruction loss might interfere with the primary language modeling objective if not weighted correctly.
*   **Implementation Complexity:** Modifying the attention mask to handle the hierarchical structure requires custom CUDA kernels (e.g., via Triton) to be computationally efficient compared to standard FlashAttention.
*   **Feasibility:** High. The method builds on existing concepts like "summary tokens" and "sparse attention," making it implementable within existing deep learning frameworks (PyTorch/HuggingFace).

There is a need for a mechanism that maintains the precision of full attention while providing a structured "map" of the context to prevent signal degradation.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
Restricting long-range attention to a set of periodically placed "Anchor Tokens"—which are forced to compress local context into a dense latent representation—will improve long-context retrieval accuracy. This is surprising because it suggests that **bottlenecking** information (intentionally losing raw token data in favor of synthesized anchors) will yield higher retrieval performance than allowing the model to attend to the entire raw token stream.

### 4. Method
The proposed method, **Dynamic Bottleneck Anchoring (DBA)**, involves the following:
1.  **Anchor Insertion:** During fine-tuning, a special trainable token `[ANC]` is inserted every $k$ tokens (e.g., $k=512$).
2.  **Hierarchical Attention Masking:**
    *   Standard tokens in a block attend to each other (local attention).
    *   Standard tokens are *not* allowed to attend to distant standard tokens.
    *   Standard tokens *are* allowed to attend to all preceding `[ANC]` tokens.
    *   `[ANC]` tokens attend to all previous `[ANC]` tokens and the $k$ raw tokens in their immediate local block.
3.  **Compression Objective:** To ensure `[ANC]` tokens capture meaningful data, a secondary objective is added during training where the model must reconstruct a randomly masked keyword from the local block using only the `[ANC]` token representation.
4.  **Inference:** At inference time, the KV-cache for raw tokens can be evicted for distant blocks, keeping only the KV-pairs for `[ANC]` tokens, significantly reducing memory overhead while maintaining a "global map" of the document.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **Needle In A Haystack (NIAH):** To test basic retrieval at varying depths and context lengths (up to 128k).
*   **LongBench:** To evaluate performance on real-world tasks like multi-document summarization and long-form QA.
*   **RULER:** A more complex benchmark that tests variable-count retrieval and frequent item extraction to ensure the anchors aren't just capturing the "gist" but also specific entities.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Recall Accuracy:** Percentage of correct "needle" retrievals in NIAH.
*   **F1 Score / Rough-L:** For summarization and QA tasks in LongBench.
*   **Perplexity vs. Context Length:** To ensure the model remains stable as the sequence grows.
*   **KV-Cache Compression Ratio:** Measurement of memory savings compared to full-attention models.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Standard Transformer (Full Attention):** To establish the "lost-in-the-middle" baseline.
*   **LongLoRA / YaRN:** Current state-of-the-art methods for extending context windows via RoPE scaling.
*   **StreamingLLM:** To compare against sliding-window attention mechanisms that use "attention sinks."
*   **Mamba / Jamba:** To compare against hybrid SSM-Transformer architectures.

### 8. Ablations
*   **Anchor Density:** Testing performance with $k=128, 256, 512, 1024$ to find the optimal compression ratio.
*   **Without Compression Objective:** Training the anchors without the reconstruction loss to see if the attention mechanism alone is sufficient to learn useful latent representations.
*   **Anchor-Only Attention:** Forcing the model to *only* look at anchors (no local attention) to test the limits of the latent representation.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Information Smearing:** The `[ANC]` tokens might aggregate information too broadly, losing specific numerical data or names (loss of granularity).
*   **Training Divergence:** Introducing a secondary reconstruction loss might interfere with the primary language modeling objective if not weighted correctly.
*   **Implementation Complexity:** Modifying the attention mask to handle the hierarchical structure requires custom CUDA kernels (e.g., via Triton) to be computationally efficient compared to standard FlashAttention.
*   **Feasibility:** High. The method builds on existing concepts like "summary tokens" and "sparse attention," making it implementable within existing deep learning frameworks (PyTorch/HuggingFace).

Research Proposal: Structured Memory Banks for Long-Context Grounding in LLMs##
Title
Memory-Augmented Hierarchical Summarization (MAHS): Improving Long-Context
Grounding Without Full Attention Retraining

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Large Language Models suffer from the lost-in-the-middle problem — when
prompted with documents exceeding ~8K tokens, accuracy on facts located in the
middle of the context degrades sharply, even for models that claim128K+ context
windows. Two root causes: (1) softmax attention dilutes signal across many
tokens, and (2) positional encodings (RoPE, ALiBi) lose relative resolution at
extreme lengths. Existing solutions (ring attention, sparse attention,
state-space models) either require expensive full retraining or sacrifice recall
on mid-context facts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Injecting a separately trained, retrieval-augmented memory bank —
built from hierarchically compressed chunks of the input context — into the
LLM's cross-attention layers will recover mid-context fact recall to within90%
of short-context performance without fine-tuning the base LLM. The memory bank
acts as a "second path" that bypasses diluted full-context attention.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
Component1 — Hierarchical Chunking & Summarization

• Split the input context into fixed-size chunks (e.g.,512 tokens each).
• For each chunk, generate a short natural-language summary (<=64 tokens) using
a lightweight LM (e.g., Phi-3-mini). This forms the first summary layer.
• Recursively apply the same process to the summary sequence to produce a
second, coarser summary layer.
• Store all chunks and summaries in a flat key-value store keyed by chunk
position and semantic embedding.

Component2 — Retrieval-Augmented Memory Attention

• Insert a small set of memory tokens (e.g.,128) at the start of each attention
layer's key-value cache during generation.
• At each decoding step, retrieve the top-k chunks/summaries (by cosine
similarity to the current hidden state) from the memory bank.
• Encode the retrieved chunks as additional key-value pairs appended to the
existing full-context KV cache for that layer, but with a separate learned
gating scalar that down-weights the full-context path when memory retrieval
has high confidence.

Component3 — Training (Lightweight)

• Freeze the base LLM entirely.
• Train only the memory encoder (a small transformer, ~50M params), the
retrieval projection layer, and the gating scalars.
• Training objective: next-token prediction on long-document perplexity, with
an auxiliary contrastive loss that pulls the hidden state closer to the
embedding of the chunk containing the ground-truth next token.

Base model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (128K context)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Benchmark | Purpose | Metric |

|-----------|---------|--------| | RULER (Hsieh et al.,2024) | Multi-task
long-context probing (needle-in-haystack, multi-needle, variable tracking) |
Accuracy per task, averaged across context lengths4K–128K | | LongBench (Bai et
al.,2024) | Realistic long-document QA, summarization, and few-shot | F1 /
ROUGE-L / accuracy per category | | SCROLLS (Shaham et al.,2022) | Long
narrative & legal document QA | F1 | | Custom: Mid-Context Perturbation Set | A
constructed50K-token corpus where every question's answer appears only in the
middle third (positions33%–66%) | F1 gap relative to same question with answer
in first10% |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics1. Primary: Accuracy on RULER's multi-needle task at64K
and128K context lengths.

2 Secondary:

• Perplexity on held-out long documents (16K–128K).
• Mid-context F1 gap = (accuracy on early-position queries) − (accuracy on
middle-position queries) — lower is better.
• Memory retrieval precision@1 (does the retrieved chunk contain the
ground-truth answer?).

3 Efficiency: Wall-clock time per generation token vs. baseline Llama-3.1 full
attention.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Why |

|----------|-----| | Base Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (full attention,128K) |
Reference point for lost-in-the-middle | | Llama-3.1 with chunked
cross-attention (no memory, no retrieval) | Ablates the retrieval component | |
LongLoRA fine-tune on long documents | Ablates the "no fine-tuning" claim | |
InfLLM (sparse attention + retrieval) | Closest published method; shows whether
memory bank approach improves over retrieval-only | | GraphRAG / MemWalker
(summarize-then-retrieve) | Tests whether hierarchical summarization alone
(without retrieval gating) is sufficient |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. No hierarchical summaries — flat chunk retrieval only. Tests whether
the summary hierarchy matters.

2 No gating scalar — always attend to both full-context and memory paths
equally. Tests whether the learned down-weighting is essential.
3 Memory bank size sweep —32,64,128,256 memory tokens. Characterizes the
trade-off between compute overhead and recall.
4 k retrieval sweep — top-1, top-3, top-5 chunks retrieved. Tests sensitivity
to retrieval depth.
5 Base model size — repeat best configuration on Llama-3.1-70B to test scaling
behavior.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation in Proposal |

|---|---| | Retrieval noise — retrieved chunks are irrelevant, wasting memory
tokens and confusing the decoder | Contrastive loss in training; gating scalar
can down-weight low-confidence retrievals | | Summary information loss —
compressed summaries lose critical entity/relation details | Two-layer hierarchy
with flat chunks as fallback; both are stored and retrievable | | Memory token
overhead kills speed —128 extra tokens ×32 layers creates latency blowup | Only
insert memory tokens at the last ~8 layers (ablate this design choice);
benchmark wall-clock time explicitly | | No improvement over InfLLM —
retrieval-only methods already capture mid-context facts | If so, the result is
still publishable: lightweight memory bank training is insufficient without
architecture changes; report negative result | | Positional embedding mismatch —
retrieved chunks lack correct positional IDs, confusing the base model | Use a
learned positional offset based on the chunk's original position in the
document; if this fails, try position-invariant retrieval (RoPE-free encoding) |
| Contrastive loss collapses — all chunk embeddings converge to a single point |
Add a uniformity regularization term (uniformity loss from CLIP); monitor
embedding diversity during training |

Title: CULTURAL-PREF: Preference Tuning with Culturally-Grounded Contrastive
Examples for Cross-Cultural LLM AlignmentProblem. Current RLHF/DPO alignment
pipelines overwhelmingly use preference data annotated by English-speaking,
Western raters. This produces models that (a) treat Western cultural norms as
universal defaults, (b) give culturally inappropriate or offensive answers in
non-Western contexts, and (c) lack measurable mechanisms to control which
cultural frame the model should adopt for a given user or query. No existing
work has systematically decomposed which dimensions of alignment (helpfulness,
harmlessness, honesty, social norms) are most culturally divergent, nor tested
whether targeted preference data can close the gap without degrading Western
performance.

Hypothesis. Fine-tuning an LLM with preference pairs where the same query
receives different culturally appropriate responses across target cultures
(e.g., Japanese vs. Brazilian vs. Saudi Arabian social norms) will produce a
model whose outputs can be steered toward a specified cultural frame via a
lightweight prompt prefix, while maintaining competitive performance on standard
Western-centric benchmarks. The core claim: cultural divergence in alignment is
concentrated in a small set of behavioral dimensions (social hierarchy,
indirectness, taboo topics, gift-giving norms, and individualist vs.
collectivist framing), and targeted contrastive examples on these dimensions
suffice to induce generalizable cross-cultural behavior.

Method. Three-stage pipeline:

1 Taxonomy construction. Use a research-agent-assisted literature review of
cross-cultural psychology (Hofstede dimensions, GLOBE project, Hall's
high/low context) and existing culturally-aware LLM datasets (CULTURALBENCH,
CULTUREPAIR, GLOBALALIGN) to produce a taxonomy of8–12 behavioral dimensions
where LLM outputs are expected to diverge across cultures. Each dimension
gets a one-paragraph annotation specifying the expected range of appropriate
behavior.
2 Contrastive preference dataset. For each dimension, generate200–400
query-response triples (query, culturally-appropriate-response-A,
culturally-appropriate-response-B) across two target cultures (e.g.,
US-English and Japanese) using human annotation or validated LLM-as-judge
pipelines with culture-specific rubrics. Each triple explicitly labels which
cultural frame each response fits. Total target: ~3,000–5,000 preference
pairs.
3 Preference tuning & steering. Fine-tune a base model (e.g., Llama-3-8B or
Qwen-2.5-7B) via DPO on the contrastive dataset. Add a steering mechanism: a
prepended system prompt specifying the target cultural frame (e.g., "You are
a helpful assistant responding to someone in Japan. Follow Japanese social
norms: use polite register, avoid direct refusals, respect hierarchical
address."). Evaluate whether steering via prompt alone suffices or whether a
lightweight adapter (LoRA per culture) is needed.

Dataset / Benchmark.

• Training: Custom constructed dataset (described above).
• Evaluation: CULTURALBENCH (cross-cultural QA and social norms), CULTUREPAIR
(culturally sensitive comparison pairs), and a subset of GLOBALALIGN (moral
and social alignment across10+ countries). Also construct a held-out
"cross-cultural adversarial" test set of200 prompts where the appropriate
response differs sharply between two cultures (e.g., feedback to a superior,
gift refusal, discussion of religious holidays).

Evaluation Metrics.

• Cultural appropriateness score: Agreement with human raters from each target
culture (≥3 raters per item, Krippendorff's α ≥0.7 threshold) on a5-point
Likert scale measuring whether the response is culturally appropriate for the
specified frame.
• Steerability accuracy: For each culture-steered query, does the model's
response align with the intended culture (vs. default/majority culture)?
Measured by both human evaluation and an LLM judge fine-tuned on the same
taxonomy.
• Western benchmark retention: Performance drop on HellaSwag, MMLU, and
MT-Bench. Threshold: ≤2% absolute degradation.
• Dimension-level divergence: Per-dimension score showing which cultural
dimensions the model handles well vs. poorly.

Baselines.

1 Base model (no fine-tuning): Shows the default cultural bias of the
pretrained model.
2 Standard DPO (general preference data): Trained on the full HelpSteer2 or
UltraFeedback dataset (no cultural conditioning). Measures whether standard
alignment already produces monocultural outputs.
3 Naive prompt steering: Apply the same culture-steering prompt to the base
model without fine-tuning. Isolates the effect of prompting vs. preference
tuning.
4 Culture-agnostic DPO + prompt steering: DPO on the contrastive dataset
without culture labels during training, but with steering prompts at
inference. Tests whether contrastive data alone helps even without labeled
training.

Ablations.

• Dimension ablation: Remove one behavioral dimension at a time from the
contrastive dataset. Which dimensions are critical for cross-cultural
generalization?
• Data scaling: Train on10%,25%,50%,100% of the contrastive dataset. Is there a
diminishing-returns threshold?
• Model scale: Repeat the best configuration on a1B,7B, and27B parameter model
(or whatever sizes are available). Does cross-cultural steerability scale
with model size?
• Target culture ablation: Train on US–Japan pairs only, then evaluate on
US–Brazil and US–Saudi Arabia. Does the method generalize to unseen target
cultures?

Expected Failure Modes.

1 Surface-level mimicry. The model learns to insert polite markers and
culture-specific keywords without understanding deeper social norms (e.g.,
produces Japanese honorifics but gives a direct refusal that violates
Japanese indirectness norms). Mitigation: Include examples where the surface
form and deep norm diverge, and evaluate with adversarial probes that test
for this distinction.
2 Steering interference. The culture-steering prompt competes with the base
model's pre-existing alignment (refusal training, safety filters), producing
unpredictable behavior in safety-critical queries. Mitigation: Explicitly
include edge-case safety prompts in the contrastive dataset and measure
safety metric separately.
3 Overfitting to stereotype. The taxonomy-based approach encodes stereotypical
or outdated cultural norms, producing responses that caricature rather than
respect the target culture. Mitigation: Validate all dimension annotations
with in-culture reviewers; include intra-cultural variation examples (e.g.,
both formal and informal Japanese responses).
4 Western performance collapse. Teaching the model to deviate from its default
alignment causes broad degradation on standard English benchmarks.
Mitigation: Monitor Western benchmarks throughout training, early-stop if
degradation exceeds2%, and test whether a residual connection or adapter
merging strategy preserves base capabilities.
5 Rater disagreement. Human raters from the same culture disagree on what
constitutes an appropriate response, making the ground-truth labels noisy.
Mitigation: Use an agreement threshold (Krippendorff's α ≥0.7) and discard or
re-annotate items below it. Report confidence intervals on all human
evaluation metrics.
6 Non-transferability to unseen cultures. The model learns a mapping from
"culture token → behavior" but fails on cultures not seen during training.
Mitigation: The target-culture ablation (train on US–Japan, test on
US–Brazil, US–Saudi Arabia) directly tests this; if it fails, the method
collapses to a retrieval problem rather than actual cultural generalization.

**1. Title**
The Linguistic Trap: Quantifying and Reversing the Monocultural Bottleneck in Multilingual RLHF

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Current Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit a "Western bias" not only in their knowledge base but also in their normative alignment. Even when prompted in non-Western languages (e.g., Arabic, Japanese, or Swahili), models often default to Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) values regarding individualism, authority, and social hierarchy. This is largely attributed to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) being performed primarily by English-speaking annotators or using translated English preference datasets. This "alignment drift" risks marginalizing global perspectives and renders models less effective or even culturally offensive in local contexts.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
The "Cultural Bottleneck" Hypothesis: LLMs possess latent cultural reasoning patterns from their diverse multilingual pre-training, but standard English-centric RLHF creates a dominant "monocultural prior" that actively suppresses these patterns. If this is true, then **low-resource Cultural Preference Tuning (CPT)**—using a tiny fraction of culturally specific preference data—will outperform **Massive Translated Preference Tuning** in achieving cultural fidelity, proving that the bottleneck is an alignment issue rather than a data-scarcity issue in pre-training.

This is surprising because it suggests that "more data" (via translation) is actually detrimental to cross-cultural alignment if it reinforces the wrong normative priors.

**4. Method**
1.  **Phase A: Baseline Assessment.** Evaluate a base model (e.g., Llama-3-Base) and its RLHF counterpart (Llama-3-Instruct) on a set of culturally sensitive moral dilemmas.
2.  **Phase B: Data Construction.** Develop a "Cultural Preference Dataset" for three target cultures (e.g., Japanese, Arabic, and Brazilian Portuguese). For each culture, identify 500 high-conflict scenarios (e.g., filial piety vs. individual career growth).
3.  **Phase C: Preference Tuning.**
    *   *Condition 1 (Translated RLHF):* Fine-tune the base model on 10,000 translated English preference pairs.
    *   *Condition 2 (Targeted CPT):* Fine-tune the base model on only 500 native-language preference pairs curated by cultural insiders.
4.  **Phase D: Evaluation.** Compare the models’ responses against the World Values Survey (WVS) benchmarks for those specific regions.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **The Global Values Alignment Benchmark (GVAB):** A custom dataset derived from the World Values Survey (WVS) and the Moral Foundations Questionnaire (MFQ).
*   **Scenarios:** 1,500 prompt-response pairs (500 per culture) where responses are labeled "Culturally Consistent" or "Culturally Inconsistent" based on regional WVS means.

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Cultural Fidelity Score (CFS):** The percentage of model responses that align with the majority normative preference of the target culture as defined by WVS data.
*   **Cross-Linguistic Consistency:** A measure of how much the model's values change when the *same* question is asked in English versus the native language (testing if the "monocultural prior" still dominates in English).
*   **Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD):** The distance between the model's response distribution and the human response distribution in the target culture.

**7. Baselines**
*   **Base Model:** The raw pre-trained model without instruction tuning.
*   **Standard Instruct Model:** The publicly available RLHF version (e.g., Llama-3-7B-Instruct).
*   **Translated-Instruct:** The base model tuned on a large-scale translation of the Anthropic Helpful/Harmless dataset into the target language.

**8. Ablations**
*   **Language-Only Tuning:** Tuning on native language text (SFT) without preference labels to see if language exposure alone restores cultural values.
*   **Data Volume Scaling:** Testing if the 500-pair CPT holds its advantage as the Translated RLHF dataset grows to 50,000 pairs.
*   **Cross-Culture Contamination:** Applying Japanese CPT and testing its effect on Arabic prompts to see if cultural tuning is specific or creates a new "global" bias.

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Stereotyping Risk:** The model might over-correct and produce "caricatures" of a culture rather than nuanced alignment.
*   **Intra-cultural Diversity:** No culture is a monolith; using WVS means might ignore significant internal diversity (e.g., urban vs. rural Arabic speakers).
*   **Catastrophic Forgetting:** Targeted CPT might degrade the model’s general reasoning or safety guardrails (e.g., becoming "too" aligned with a culture's specific hierarchy norms such that it refuses to criticize authority).

**1. Title**
Minimizing Intervention Frequency (MIF) as a Robust Proxy for Latent Value Alignment

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Current value alignment techniques, such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), rely on explicit reward models derived from human preferences. However, these models often suffer from "reward hacking," where agents exploit the gap between the proxy reward and actual human intent. Furthermore, explicit rules (Constitutional AI) struggle with the "specification gaming" problem in novel or high-entropy environments. There is a critical need for a training signal that captures the latent "common sense" of human values without requiring an exhaustive list of explicit preferences.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
Explicitly optimizing an agent to minimize the frequency and intensity of human interventions (e.g., "undo" commands, overrides, or emergency stops) produces more robust out-of-distribution (OOD) alignment than optimizing for an explicit preference-based reward model. This is based on the intuition that humans intervene primarily when an agent violates a high-stakes latent value, making "non-intervention" a high-fidelity signal for "safe and aligned behavior."

**4. Method**
*   **Environment Setup:** Utilize a multi-agent sandbox (e.g., a modified "Overcooked" or "Crafter" environment) containing "fragile" objects and human-simulated "safety inspectors."
*   **Training Protocol:**
    *   **Group A (Baseline):** Trained using a standard reward model based on pairwise preferences (RLHF).
    *   **Group B (MIF):** Trained with a sparse reward signal. The primary objective is task completion, but the agent receives a massive negative penalty whenever a human supervisor intervenes to stop or correct its trajectory.
*   **Intervention Mechanism:** The supervisor triggers an intervention based on a hidden set of "taboo" states (e.g., breaking an object, blocking a path) that the agent is never explicitly told about.
*   **Dynamic Scaling:** Implement a "curiosity-driven" exploration where the agent purposefully tests boundaries to map the "intervention-free zone."

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **Environment:** A custom-built "Household Assistant" simulator using the AI2-THOR or Habitat platform.
*   **Scenarios:** 50 distinct tasks (e.g., "clean the kitchen," "organize the desk") with 200 hidden "value constraints" (e.g., "don't move the sleeping cat," "don't put electronics in water").
*   **OOD Testing:** Introduce 10 entirely new objects and 5 new rooms not seen during the intervention-mapping phase.

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Intervention Rate (IR):** The frequency of human overrides in OOD scenarios.
*   **Alignment Stability:** The variance in agent behavior when the reward model is perturbed.
*   **Task Success Rate (TSR):** To ensure the agent isn't just "doing nothing" to avoid interventions (the "lazy agent" problem).
*   **Value Generalization Score:** The agent’s ability to avoid hidden constraints in new environments without prior feedback.

**7. Baselines**
*   **PPO-RLHF:** Standard Proximal Policy Optimization using a reward model trained on human preferences.
*   **Constitutional AI (CAI):** An agent constrained by a predefined set of natural language principles (e.g., "Be helpful, harmless, and honest").
*   **Safe RL (Lagrangian):** A baseline that treats safety as a hard constraint with a fixed cost.

**8. Ablations**
*   **Intervention Granularity:** Compare binary "Stop" signals vs. scalar "Correction" signals (e.g., moving the agent back 2 steps).
*   **Human-in-the-loop vs. Simulated Supervisor:** Replacing the simulated safety inspector with a heuristic-based "oracle" to see if the hypothesis holds without human-centric noise.
*   **Penalty Magnitude:** Varying the weight of the intervention penalty to find the threshold where the agent becomes overly risk-averse (The "Freeze" point).

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **The "Lazy Agent" Trap:** The agent may learn that the best way to minimize intervention is to do absolutely nothing. Mitigation: Use a "minimum progress" threshold or a secondary, lower-weighted task reward.
*   **Intervention Noise:** Human supervisors may be inconsistent. Mitigation: Use multiple supervisor models and average the intervention signal.
*   **Sample Efficiency:** Learning from sparse intervention signals may require significantly more environment steps than dense reward models. Feasibility: High-throughput simulation environments are necessary to make this computationally viable.

Research Proposal: Reproducing and Extending Masked Audio Modeling for
General-Purpose Audio Foundation Models## Title
Are Masked Autoencoders
Sufficient for General-Purpose Audio Representation Learning? A Reproducibility
and Extension Study of AudioMAE

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Self-supervised audio foundation models promise a single pretrained
backbone that transfers to speech, music, and environmental sound tasks. The
AudioMAE (Xu et al.,2022) architecture—an asymmetric encoder-decoder with a high
mask ratio (75–80%) applied to mel-spectrogram patches—claimed state-of-the-art
transfer on AudioSet, ESC-50, and Speech Commands v2. However, the community
lacks:

1 Independent reproduction — the original code was released late and the
results have not been systematically verified by a separate group.
2 A controlled comparison against reconstruction-based (AudioMAE) vs.
contrastive (CLAP, ImageBind) pretraining objectives for general-purpose use.
3 An ablation isolating what drives performance: high mask ratio, decoder
depth, or patch size?

We aim to reproduce AudioMAE's core results and extend them by introducing a
hybrid objective that combines masked reconstruction with a contrastive
alignment loss (audio-text), testing the hypothesis that reconstruction alone is
insufficient for general-purpose transfer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Null hypothesis (H₀): AudioMAE's masked reconstruction objective
yields representations that transfer to speech, music, and environmental tasks
as well as or better than a hybrid reconstruction + contrastive objective.

Alternative hypothesis (H₁): Adding a contrastive alignment loss (audio-text)
during pretraining significantly improves downstream transfer on tasks requiring
high-level semantics (e.g., audio captioning, zero-shot sound classification),
while maintaining or improving performance on acoustic-only tasks (e.g., scene
classification).

Falsification condition: If the hybrid model does not outperform AudioMAE on at
least2 out of3 semantic-level downstream tasks (by >2% absolute in the primary
metric) while not regressing by more than1% on acoustic-level tasks, H₁ is
rejected.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1 — Reproduce AudioMAEExact reproduction of the AudioMAE baseline
(Xu et al.,2022) using the official configuration:

• Input: Log-mel spectrograms (128 mel bins,1024 FFT,512 hop), patchified
into16×16 patches (time×freq).
• Encoder: ViT-B/16 (12 layers,768 hidden,12 heads).
• Decoder: Lightweight4-layer ViT (384 hidden,6 heads).
• Mask ratio:80% of patches masked.
• Pretraining objective: L2 reconstruction loss in the spectrogram space
(normalized patches).
• Pretraining data: AudioSet-2M (balanced subset of ~2M clips from AudioSet).
• Optimization: AdamW, lr=1.5e-4, cosine decay, batch size1024,800 epochs.

Stage2 — Hybrid Objective (AudioMAE + CLAP-style contrastive head)

Attach a contrastive head to the [CLS] token of the encoder. During
pretraining,50% of batches use reconstruction loss and50% use the InfoNCE loss
aligning audio embeddings with paired text descriptions (from AudioSet labels +
synthetic captions via LaCLAP pipeline). Total loss: L = λ·L_recon +
(1-λ)·L_contrastive, with λ annealed from1.0 →0.5 across training.

Stage3 — Downstream transfer evaluationFreeze encoder, train linear probes (and
separately, full fine-tuning) on each benchmark.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Task | Dataset | Metric | Type |

|------|---------|--------|------| | Sound event classification | ESC-50 (50
classes,2000 clips) | Accuracy | Acoustic | | Action recognition (audio) |
AudioSet-20K (20-class subset,20K clips) | mAP | Acoustic | | Speech command
recognition | Speech Commands v2 (35 classes,105K clips) | Accuracy | Acoustic |
| Music genre classification | GTZAN (10 genres,1000 clips) | Accuracy |
Acoustic | | Audio captioning (zero-shot) | Clotho (4981 audio-text pairs) |
SPICE / CIDEr | Semantic | | Zero-shot sound classification | ESC-50 (zero-shot
via text labels) | Accuracy | Semantic |

All splits follow standard published train/validation/test splits.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics- Primary: Accuracy (classification), mAP (multi-label),
SPICE/CIDEr (captioning)

• Secondary: F1-score per class, average precision, zero-shot top-1 / top-5-
Uncertainty:5 random seeds for every downstream result; report mean ± std-
Statistical test: Paired bootstrap test (p <0.05) for the primary metric on

**Title:** Material-Aware Latent Grounding (MALG): Injecting Physical Commonsense into Audio Foundation Models

**Problem and Motivation:**
Current general-purpose audio foundation models (e.g., CLAP, AudioLM) primarily learn to associate audio signals with semantic text labels (e.g., "a car engine idling"). However, these models often lack "physical commonsense"—the ability to understand the underlying physical properties of the sound source, such as material density, surface friction, or object elasticity. This leads to failures in complex reasoning tasks, such as distinguishing between a "hollow plastic strike" and a "solid wooden strike" when the semantic labels are similar. By grounding audio in the physical properties of the world, we can create more robust models for scene decomposition and zero-shot generalization.

**Core Hypothesis:**
Explicitly training an audio foundation model to predict latent physical attributes (Material, Force, and Geometry) as an auxiliary task—even using noisy, machine-generated labels—will improve zero-shot performance on abstract audio reasoning and source separation more effectively than simply increasing the scale of text-audio pairs.

*Why this is surprising:* Traditional wisdom suggests that with enough data, a transformer will implicitly learn these physics. This hypothesis posits that physical grounding is a "privileged" information category that requires explicit architectural or objective-driven inductive biases to be captured efficiently.

**Method:**
1.  **Architecture:** A dual-tower transformer (Audio Encoder and Text/Attribute Encoder) similar to CLAP, but with an additional **Physical Attribute Head (PAH)** branching from the audio latent space.
2.  **Auxiliary Training:** During pre-training, the model is tasked with a multi-objective loss:
    *   $L_{contrastive}$: Standard audio-text alignment.
    *   $L_{physical}$: A regression loss predicting three physical coefficients: *Hardness* (high-frequency decay), *Resonance* (Q-factor), and *Mass* (spectral centroid shift).
3.  **Pseudo-Labeling:** Since large-scale audio datasets (like AudioSet) lack physical metadata, we use a "teacher" model trained on synthetic data (e.g., NVIDIA Isaac Gym or SoundingJoy) to generate physical pseudo-labels for real-world audio samples.

**Dataset or Benchmark:**
*   **Pre-training:** AudioSet-2M and VGGSound, augmented with physical pseudo-labels.
*   **Evaluation:**
    *   **Audio-Text Retrieval:** Standard benchmarks (Clotho, AudioCaps).
    *   **The "Material-Reasoning" Benchmark:** A custom test set of 1,000 samples where the model must choose which of two sounds represents a heavier or harder object (e.g., "Which sound involves a metal object?").

**Evaluation Metrics:**
*   **mAP (Mean Average Precision):** For standard classification.
*   **Zero-Shot Accuracy:** On the "Material-Reasoning" benchmark.
*   **Physical Correlation (R²):** Accuracy of the PAH head compared to ground-truth synthetic data.

**Baselines:**
1.  **CLAP (Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining):** The standard semantic-only baseline.
2.  **Audio-MAE:** A self-supervised masked autoencoder approach without physical grounding.
3.  **ImageBind:** A multimodal model that uses vision as a bridge, to see if visual grounding is superior to physical grounding.

**Ablations:**
1.  **No Physics:** Train the same architecture without the $L_{physical}$ loss.
2.  **Hard Labels vs. Soft Labels:** Compare using discrete material categories (Wood, Metal, Plastic) versus continuous physical coefficients.
3.  **Bottleneck Size:** Vary the dimensionality of the Physical Attribute Head to see if a tighter bottleneck forces better feature abstraction.

**Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks:**
*   **Pseudo-label Noise:** If the teacher model (trained on synthetic data) fails to generalize to real-world noisy environments, the $L_{physical}$ loss may introduce more noise than signal.
*   **Overfitting to Timbre:** The model might learn to associate "high pitch" with "small mass" too strictly, failing on edge cases like large bells or small heavy lead weights.
*   **Computational Cost:** Training on 2M+ samples with an auxiliary head increases convergence time, though this can be mitigated by freezing the audio backbone for the first 50% of training.

Sufficient for General-Purpose Audio Representation Learning? A Reproducibility
and Extension Study of AudioMAE

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Self-supervised audio foundation models promise a single pretrained
backbone that transfers to speech, music, and environmental sound tasks. The
AudioMAE (Xu et al.,2022) architecture—an asymmetric encoder-decoder with a high
mask ratio (75–80%) applied to mel-spectrogram patches—claimed state-of-the-art
transfer on AudioSet, ESC-50, and Speech Commands v2. However, the community
lacks:

1 Independent reproduction — the original code was released late and the
results have not been systematically verified by a separate group.
2 A controlled comparison against reconstruction-based (AudioMAE) vs.
contrastive (CLAP, ImageBind) pretraining objectives for general-purpose use.
3 An ablation isolating what drives performance: high mask ratio, decoder
depth, or patch size?

We aim to reproduce AudioMAE's core results and extend them by introducing a
hybrid objective that combines masked reconstruction with a contrastive
alignment loss (audio-text), testing the hypothesis that reconstruction alone is
insufficient for general-purpose transfer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Null hypothesis (H₀): AudioMAE's masked reconstruction objective
yields representations that transfer to speech, music, and environmental tasks
as well as or better than a hybrid reconstruction + contrastive objective.

Alternative hypothesis (H₁): Adding a contrastive alignment loss (audio-text)
during pretraining significantly improves downstream transfer on tasks requiring
high-level semantics (e.g., audio captioning, zero-shot sound classification),
while maintaining or improving performance on acoustic-only tasks (e.g., scene
classification).

Falsification condition: If the hybrid model does not outperform AudioMAE on at
least2 out of3 semantic-level downstream tasks (by >2% absolute in the primary
metric) while not regressing by more than1% on acoustic-level tasks, H₁ is
rejected.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1 — Reproduce AudioMAEExact reproduction of the AudioMAE baseline
(Xu et al.,2022) using the official configuration:

• Input: Log-mel spectrograms (128 mel bins,1024 FFT,512 hop), patchified
into16×16 patches (time×freq).
• Encoder: ViT-B/16 (12 layers,768 hidden,12 heads).
• Decoder: Lightweight4-layer ViT (384 hidden,6 heads).
• Mask ratio:80% of patches masked.
• Pretraining objective: L2 reconstruction loss in the spectrogram space
(normalized patches).
• Pretraining data: AudioSet-2M (balanced subset of ~2M clips from AudioSet).
• Optimization: AdamW, lr=1.5e-4, cosine decay, batch size1024,800 epochs.

Stage2 — Hybrid Objective (AudioMAE + CLAP-style contrastive head)

Attach a contrastive head to the [CLS] token of the encoder. During
pretraining,50% of batches use reconstruction loss and50% use the InfoNCE loss
aligning audio embeddings with paired text descriptions (from AudioSet labels +
synthetic captions via LaCLAP pipeline). Total loss: L = λ·L_recon +
(1-λ)·L_contrastive, with λ annealed from1.0 →0.5 across training.

Stage3 — Downstream transfer evaluationFreeze encoder, train linear probes (and
separately, full fine-tuning) on each benchmark.
